stem: A 65-year-old heavy smoker is coming for a general examination.. What is the best screening test for him?
why_right: A 65-year-old man who is a heavy smoker fits the target group for abdominal aortic aneurysm screening: a one-time abdominal ultrasound for men aged 65 to 75 who have ever smoked. Smoking is the strongest modifiable risk factor for AAA, so the smoking clue points to AAA as the best screening test here.
why_wrong_block:
A. Routine osteoporosis (DEXA) screening targets women aged 65 or older (or younger postmenopausal women at risk); in men the evidence for routine screening is insufficient.
B. Colon cancer screening is age based (average risk 45 to 75) and applies regardless of smoking; it is reasonable for him, but the decisive smoking clue in a 65-year-old man points to AAA as the best answer.
key_concept:
Screening triggered by age plus risk factor:
  • Man 65 to 75 who has ever smoked: one-time abdominal ultrasound for AAA
  • Heavy smoker aged 50 to 80: annual low-dose CT for lung cancer
  • Woman 65 or older: DEXA for osteoporosis
  • Everyone 45 to 75: colorectal cancer screening
exam_pearl: If low-dose chest CT (lung cancer) is offered for a heavy smoker, it competes strongly; with only these options, male + 65 + smoker = AAA ultrasound.

stem: A 50-year-old man with no past medical history presents for a routine visit. He does not smoke, and is not taking any medications. Which of the following conditions should be screened for at this time?
why_right: An average-risk man of 50 years with no history is squarely inside the colorectal cancer screening window, which starts at 45 (choose 50 if 45 is not offered). Colorectal screening is a firm, universal recommendation for both sexes at this age, so it is the condition that should be screened for now.
why_wrong_block:
B. Breast cancer: routine screening (mammography) is for women; there is no population screening for breast cancer in an average-risk man.
C. Prostate cancer: PSA screening is not a routine 'should screen' test; it is an individual shared decision, mainly from 55 to 69 years. It would be the answer only if the question asked what to discuss with him.
key_concept:
Colorectal cancer screening starts at 45 (or 50 if 45 is absent) for average-risk adults.
  • Colonoscopy every 10 years
  • CT colonography or flexible sigmoidoscopy every 5 years
  • FOBT/FIT yearly; positive result means colonoscopy
  • PSA: shared decision, not routine screening
  • Mammography: women only
exam_pearl: In a 50-year-old man the only universal cancer screen is colorectal; PSA is a discussion, not a mandate.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Separate 'Q:' variant listed under 814.

stem: Female young age, her mother developed endomtrial ca, she had intramenstural bleeding and since the she is worried that she has cancer. Her friend told her to do examination Physical ex is normal Pap smear is normal Asking what stage of prevention she is at (almost like this)
why_right: She has no diagnosed disease; the physical examination and Pap smear are done to detect or exclude cancer early (her worry was triggered by intermenstrual bleeding and her mother's endometrial cancer). Early detection and prompt treatment, whether by screening or early diagnostic workup, is secondary prevention, and a normal result does not change the level of the action.
why_wrong_block:
A. Primordial: prevents risk factors from emerging in the first place (e.g., policies promoting healthy lifestyle in a population); no test is done on an individual.
B. Primary: prevents disease before it starts in a healthy person, e.g., HPV vaccination or health education; a Pap smear detects disease rather than preventing its onset.
C. Tertiary: limits complications and disability in established disease (e.g., rehabilitation after cancer treatment); she has no diagnosed disease.
key_concept:
Levels of prevention are defined by what the action does, not by who the patient is.
  • Primordial: stop risk factors appearing (population level)
  • Primary: stop disease starting (vaccine, education)
  • Secondary: detect early and treat (screening, Pap smear, mammogram)
  • Tertiary: limit disability in established disease (rehab)
exam_pearl: HPV vaccine is primary; Pap smear is secondary, even when the result is normal.

stem: Two researchers are conducting a clinical trial to test a new drug intended to improve nutritional status in malnourished children. They recruit participants only from specialized malnutrition rehabilitation centers (facilities dedicated exclusively to the treatment and nutritional rehabilitation of malnourished children). The trial shows significant improvement in nutritional outcomes among the participants. What is the most important methodological error/bias in this study?
OptD: Information bias / Measurement bias / Observer bias
highlight_terms_source: recruit participants only from specialized malnutrition rehabilitation centers
why_right: Participants were recruited only from specialized malnutrition rehabilitation centers, so the study population is not representative of malnourished children in general (those centers differ in severity, care and co-interventions). A flaw in how participants are chosen is selection bias, and it limits how far the 'significant improvement' can be generalized.
why_wrong_block:
B. Recall bias: arises when participants remember past exposures differently (classically in case-control studies); this trial measures outcomes prospectively, not from memory.
C. Confounding: a third variable linked to both exposure and outcome distorts the association; it would be the answer if the stem highlighted an unbalanced factor such as the centers' intensive feeding, not the recruitment site itself.
D. Information/measurement/observer bias: errors in how outcomes are measured or recorded (e.g., unblinded assessors); the stem describes nothing about measurement.
key_concept:
Identify bias by the stage of the study where it enters.
  • Choosing participants: selection bias
  • Remembering exposure: recall bias
  • Measuring/recording data: information (observer) bias
  • Third variable: confounding
exam_pearl: The stem's emphasis on WHERE participants were recruited points to selection bias.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Original typed recall (options Selection bias / Recell bias / Confoding) highlights Selection bias; option D noted as a common example in the options.

stem: 70-year-old male with hypertension 172/85 with cholesterol i think 6 and non smoker,calculate Cardiovascular risk?
why_right: This recall's key is the highest band (>30%), read from the attached New Zealand cardiovascular risk chart, which gives a 5-year CVD risk from sex, age, diabetes, smoking, systolic BP and the TC:HDL ratio. Age 70 is the top age block and a systolic BP of 172 puts him in the top BP row; the recall takes 'cholesterol 6' as the cholesterol column and reads the cell as the top colour band despite him being a non-smoker.
why_wrong_block:
A. 16 to 19: a lower band that fits a younger man or one with lower systolic BP and cholesterol ratio; age 70 with SBP above 170 moves him well above this.
B. 20 to 24: would fit if systolic BP or cholesterol ratio were lower; the combination here is at the top of the chart.
C. 25 to 29: the adjacent band; the recall's chart reading places the 70-year-old with SBP over 170 in the highest category instead.
key_concept:
Chart-based CVD risk: locate the cell, do not calculate.
  • Pick the panel: sex, diabetes, smoking
  • Pick the age block (70 is the top block)
  • Row: systolic BP; column: TC:HDL ratio (not total cholesterol)
  • Read the colour band (5-year risk)
  • Age and SBP are the heaviest drivers
exam_pearl: Age and systolic BP dominate the chart: an elderly man with SBP over 170 lands in the top bands even without smoking.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Compiler attached the NZ cardiovascular risk chart (5-year CVD risk by age, sex, smoking, diabetes, SBP and TC:HDL ratio) below the question.

stem: During a school health program, a female student is noted to have low vision. She is referred to an ophthalmologist, where a refractive error is confirmed, and corrective glasses are prescribed This scenario represents which level of prevention?
why_right: The low vision was found through a school health program, that is a screening activity, and the refractive error was then confirmed and corrected. Detecting an existing condition early and treating it before it causes further harm (here, poor school performance) is secondary prevention.
why_wrong_block:
A. Primordial: prevents risk factors from arising at population level (e.g., policies on screen time or outdoor play); nothing here prevents a risk factor.
B. Primary: prevents the condition before it occurs (e.g., education, vitamin A supplementation); the refractive error already exists.
D. Tertiary: rehabilitation to limit disability from established, complicated disease (e.g., low-vision aids for irreversible vision loss); glasses after screening detection is early correction, not rehabilitation.
key_concept:
Screening plus early treatment = secondary prevention.
  • Primordial: prevent risk factors
  • Primary: prevent onset
  • Secondary: early detection (school vision screening, Pap, mammogram) and prompt treatment
  • Tertiary: reduce disability (rehab, low-vision services)
exam_pearl: The trigger words 'school health program' and 'noted' mean screening, so secondary prevention.

stem: researcher want to assess the relationship btw birth weight and cognitive function r= +0.8 What is the interpretation of correlation coefficient? ( 100 sure)
OptB: Inc Weight birth causes cognitive function to be low
OptC: Inc Weight birth increase cognitive development
why_right: An r of +0.8 is a strong positive correlation: as birth weight rises, cognitive function tends to rise too. Option C is the only one that captures the positive direction, so it is the key.
why_wrong_block:
A. Inverse relation: would need a negative r (e.g., −0.8); the sign here is positive.
B. Higher birth weight causing low cognitive function: wrong direction (that would be a negative r) and correlation never proves causation.
D. No relation: fits r close to 0; 0.8 is far from zero.
key_concept:
Correlation coefficient r ranges from −1 to +1.
  • Sign = direction (positive: both rise together; negative: inverse)
  • Size = strength (near 1 strong, near 0 none)
  • r measures linear association only
  • Correlation does not prove causation
exam_pearl: Pick the option that matches the sign and strength of r; 'causes' wording is a trap when a non-causal option exists.

stem: researcher want to assess the relationship btw birth weight and cognitive function r= +0.8 What is the interpretation of correlation coefficient? ( 100 sure)
OptB: wight birth little increase cognitive Development
OptC: wight birth commonly increase cognitive Development
why_right: This recall's key is B: r = +0.8 shows a positive association, so higher birth weight goes with higher cognitive development. The source's reasoning is that r describes how tightly the points follow a line, not how much cognitive function changes per unit of birth weight (that is the regression slope), so the actual size of the increase may be small.
why_wrong_block:
A. Inverse relation: would require a negative r; +0.8 is positive.
C. 'Commonly increase': describes a strong, consistent positive relation; it fails in this key only because the recall treats the magnitude of change as unknown or small.
key_concept:
Correlation coefficient: sign = direction, magnitude = strength.
  • ±0.7 to 1: strong
  • ±0.3 to 0.7: moderate
  • below ±0.3: weak
  • r does not give the size of change (slope)
  • r does not prove causation
exam_pearl: Same stem as the 4-option version: there the key is simply 'increase'; check which option describes a strong positive relation.

stem: Country conduct study of maternal mortality found there is 450 maternal death due to complication of pregnancy and childbirth , and there is in the same year 200,000 life birth. Which of the following is representing maternity mortality rate?
why_right: Maternal mortality is expressed per 100,000 live births: 450 deaths ÷ 200,000 live births × 100,000 = 225 per 100,000 live births. The deaths counted are those due to complications of pregnancy and childbirth, exactly as the stem gives.
why_wrong_block:
B. 450 per 100,000: uses the raw death count as if there were only 100,000 births; the births were 200,000, so the figure must be halved.
C. 450 per 200,000: numerically the same proportion but not expressed on the standard base of 100,000 live births, so it is not the reported indicator.
D. 0.450%: arithmetic error; 450 ÷ 200,000 is 0.225%, and the indicator is not given as a percentage.
key_concept:
Maternal mortality = maternal deaths ÷ live births × 100,000.
  • Numerator: deaths from pregnancy/childbirth complications
  • Denominator: live births in the same year
  • Base: 100,000 live births
  • Strictly, per live births is the maternal mortality ratio; the true rate uses women of reproductive age, but exams usually call both 'rate'
  • Infant mortality uses a base of 1,000 live births
exam_pearl: Always convert to the standard base: maternal per 100,000 live births, infant per 1,000.

stem: Q similar to this but another disease 50 case of meningococcal meningitis 5 died What is the case fatality
why_right: Case fatality rate = deaths from the disease ÷ number of cases × 100. Here 5 deaths ÷ 50 cases × 100 = 10%.
why_wrong_block:
A. 5%: results from dividing deaths by 100 instead of the 50 cases.
C. 15%: no correct arithmetic from 5 and 50 gives this value.
D. 20%: would need 10 deaths among 50 cases (or 5 among 25).
key_concept:
Case fatality rate measures disease severity (lethality).
  • CFR = deaths from disease ÷ cases of that disease × 100
  • Denominator is cases, not the whole population
  • Mortality rate uses the total population as denominator
exam_pearl: If the denominator is the population rather than the cases, you are calculating mortality, not case fatality.

stem: A 60-year-old patient with controlled Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus (DM) has missed their last two scheduled appointments at the diabetes clinic. Which of the following IOM domains of quality will help the patient to adhere to his appointments?
highlight_terms_source: missed their last two scheduled appointments
why_right: Missed appointments by a patient with controlled diabetes is an adherence and engagement problem. Patient-centeredness means care that respects the patient's preferences, needs and values (e.g., convenient scheduling, involving him in decisions, addressing barriers), which is what improves attendance.
why_wrong_block:
B. Timeliness: reducing waits and harmful delays for those who seek care; it fits a question about long waiting lists or delayed results, not a patient who does not come.
C. Efficiency: avoiding waste of equipment, supplies, ideas and energy; it fits a cost or duplication scenario.
D. Safety: avoiding injury from care meant to help (e.g., medication errors, falls); nothing here involves harm from care.
key_concept:
IOM six domains of quality (STEEEP).
  • Safe: avoid harm from care
  • Timely: reduce waits and delays
  • Effective: evidence-based, avoid under/overuse
  • Efficient: avoid waste
  • Equitable: same quality regardless of personal characteristics
  • Patient-centered: respect preferences, needs and values
exam_pearl: Adherence, engagement and the patient's own needs point to patient-centered; waiting time points to timely.

stem: A study about covid vaccine was conducted, 10000 participants were divided into 2 groups randomly, the first group will take covid vaccine and the second group will take placebo. What is the type of study?
why_right: The investigator assigned the exposure (vaccine vs placebo) and did so randomly across two groups, then compared outcomes. Assignment of the intervention by the researcher makes it an experimental (interventional) study, and random allocation with a placebo control makes it a randomized controlled clinical trial.
why_wrong_block:
A. Cohort study: observational; people are grouped by an exposure they already have or chose (e.g. vaccinated by personal choice) and followed forward. Here the researcher assigned the vaccine, so it is not observational.
B. Case-control study: starts from outcome (people with COVID vs without) and looks back at past exposure. This study starts from exposure and moves forward.
C. Cross-sectional study: exposure and outcome measured at one point in time (a survey of prevalence). There is no follow-up and no intervention here.
key_concept:
Who decides the exposure? Investigator = experimental (trial); nature/patient = observational.
  • Random allocation + control/placebo = RCT
  • Exposure groups followed forward = cohort (incidence, RR)
  • Start from cases vs controls, look back = case-control (OR)
  • Single time point = cross-sectional (prevalence)
exam_pearl: The words "randomly divided" and "placebo" settle it; a cohort never has the researcher handing out the exposure.

stem: In a village, there were 50 deaths among children under five years of age out of a total population of 2,000 children under five. Calculate the mortality rate?
why_right: Mortality rate = deaths ÷ population at risk × 1,000. Here 50 deaths ÷ 2,000 children under five = 0.025, which is 25 per 1,000 children under five.
why_wrong_block: A. 50 per 1,000 would need 50 deaths in a population of 1,000 (it puts the deaths over 1,000 without dividing by the actual 2,000 at risk).
key_concept:
Rate = events ÷ population at risk in the same period, scaled (per 1,000).
  • Here: 50 ÷ 2,000 × 1,000 = 25
  • Denominator must be the population at risk (children under five), not total village population
  • Note: the standard under-five mortality rate (U5MR) uses live births as denominator; this recall uses the stated population
exam_pearl: Always divide by the population at risk first, then scale to 1,000; do not just read off the death count.

stem: A female patient with a history of HTN, DM, and DLP, with a Fhx of cardiac disease, reports a diet high in processed foods, red meat, and fried foods. Which of the following is the most appropriate dietary advice?
OptA: Reduce or increase fat intake (I don't remember exactly)
OptD: Mediterranean diet focusing on vegetables, fruits, whole grains,..
highlight_terms_source: processed foods, red meat, and fried foods
why_right: She has several cardiovascular risk factors (HTN, DM, DLP, family history) plus a diet rich in processed foods, red meat and fried foods. A Mediterranean pattern (vegetables, fruits, whole grains, legumes, olive oil, fish, limited red and processed meat) has proven benefit on cardiovascular events and improves blood pressure, glycaemia and lipids, so it is the most appropriate dietary advice.
why_wrong_block:
A. A vague change in total fat is not the advice; the quality of fat and the whole dietary pattern matter more than simply raising or lowering fat amount.
B. A high protein diet centred on meat increases saturated fat and red/processed meat, worsening her lipid and cardiovascular risk.
C. Continuing a processed, red meat and fried food diet ignores a major modifiable risk factor in a high risk patient.
key_concept:
High cardiovascular risk patient: recommend a heart-healthy dietary pattern, not single nutrient tweaks.
  • Mediterranean or DASH style eating
  • More vegetables, fruits, whole grains, legumes, nuts, fish, olive oil
  • Less red and processed meat, fried foods, refined carbohydrates, salt
  • Combine with regular exercise (at least 30 min most days)
exam_pearl: "Focus on meat" or "continue the same" are never right for a patient with HTN, DM and DLP; pick the whole-pattern diet.

stem: Patient planning to go for Hajj and wants to receive the meningococcal vaccine. When should the vaccine be administered?
why_right: The quadrivalent (ACYW135) meningococcal vaccine is mandatory for all Hajj pilgrims, and Saudi regulations require it to be given at least 10 days before arrival so that protective antibodies have time to develop. Hence the recall's key: 10 days before Hajj.
why_wrong_block:
A. "Now" is not the specified timing; the rule is defined by the 10 day lead time before arrival (the certificate must also still be valid at the time of Hajj).
C. Not required is wrong: meningococcal vaccination is a mandatory Hajj entry requirement for pilgrims from any country.
D. On arrival is too late, as immunity would not be established during the Hajj; on-arrival measures are chemoprophylaxis (e.g. single dose ciprofloxacin) for pilgrims from the African meningitis belt, not the primary vaccine.
key_concept:
Hajj meningococcal rule: ACYW135 vaccine, mandatory for all, given ≥10 days before arrival.
  • Required for pilgrims from any country
  • From African meningitis belt: vaccine plus chemoprophylaxis on arrival
  • Yellow fever and polio required only for travellers from at-risk countries
exam_pearl: Vaccine = before (≥10 days); ciprofloxacin = on arrival for meningitis belt pilgrims.

stem: In a village, there are usually about 10 cases of gastroenteritis per week. Suddenly, the number of cases increased significantly, and all affected individuals ate at the same restaurant (not sure). What is the most appropriate health response?
OptA: Close the restaurant immediately without investigation
OptB: Wait for more cases before starting an investigation
OptD: Consider it related to something else
key_concept:
Outbreak = more cases than expected for place and time; respond with a structured investigation.
  • Steps: verify diagnosis, confirm outbreak (compare with baseline)
  • Case definition and case finding
  • Descriptive epidemiology (time, place, person), then hypothesis
  • Analytic study to test it
  • Control measures (may start early if source is obvious), communicate findings
exam_pearl: A significant rise above baseline with a common exposure means investigate now; closing without evidence or waiting for more cases are classic traps.
compiler_note:
Compiler note: Recaller note on D (Arabic): doesn't remember the exact option, but it meant these are ordinary cases unrelated to poisoning from the restaurant. No answer marked.
⚠ The source marked no answer for this recall (page and next page checked).

stem: question about food poisoning of 13 doctors out of the 50 staff at the hospital, after investigation we found that they all ate at the hospital restaurant. so what is the first step in this outbreak?
OptA: close the restaurant and do health reassessment or something like this
OptB: check what did the infected eat?
highlight_terms_source: food poisoning of 13 doctors out of the 50 staff
all ate at the hospital restaurant
key_concept:
Food-borne outbreak: confirm cases, then a food history to find the vehicle; control measures to protect others may run in parallel.
  • Verify diagnosis and that an outbreak exists (13 of 50 ill)
  • Case definition, interview cases and non-cases on foods eaten
  • Compare attack rates per food item to find the culprit
  • Sample food, inspect kitchen and food handlers
  • Stop the source once identified
exam_pearl: Read the verb: "first step in investigating" favours a food history; "first action to prevent more cases" favours stopping exposure.

stem: saudi girl or family not sure came to clinic, want to travel to kenya, her routine vaccination is up to date, what vaccine should be given?
OptC: no need, her routine vac is enough
highlight_terms_source: routine vaccination is up to date
why_right: This recall's key is the meningococcal vaccine, reasoning that travel to sub-Saharan Africa carries meningococcal risk. In this version yellow fever is not among the options, so of the listed choices meningococcal is the only travel vaccine offered, while malaria has no routine travel vaccine and routine immunisation alone does not cover travel-specific risks.
why_wrong_block:
A. Malaria: prevention for travellers is chemoprophylaxis plus bite avoidance, not a travel vaccine; malaria vaccines are used for children living in endemic areas.
C. Routine vaccines are not enough for travel to East Africa; travel-specific vaccines must be considered based on the destination.
key_concept:
Travel to Kenya: think destination-specific vaccines beyond routine ones.
  • Yellow fever: Kenya is a yellow fever risk country (recommended for most travellers)
  • Malaria: chemoprophylaxis, not a vaccine
  • Meningococcal: mandatory for Hajj/Umrah; recommended for the African meningitis belt
  • Also consider typhoid and hepatitis A
exam_pearl: When yellow fever appears as an option for travel to Kenya, it is the answer (see the paired card with option D).

stem: saudi girl or family not sure came to clinic, want to travel to kenya, her routine vaccination is up to date, what vaccine should be given?
OptC: no need, her routine vac is enough
highlight_terms_source: routine vaccination is up to date
why_right: Kenya lies in the yellow fever endemic zone of Africa, so a traveller whose routine vaccines are up to date still needs the destination-specific yellow fever vaccine. It is a single live attenuated dose that should be given at least 10 days before travel to be valid, and the certificate is also checked on return or onward travel from a risk country.
why_wrong_block:
A. Malaria is prevented in travellers by chemoprophylaxis and mosquito bite avoidance, not by a travel vaccine.
B. Meningococcal vaccine is the key answer for Hajj/Umrah or travel to the Sahel meningitis belt; Kenya is only at the eastern edge of the extended belt, so it is not the main destination-specific vaccine here.
C. Routine immunisation does not include yellow fever, so it does not cover the destination risk in Kenya.
key_concept:
Destination drives travel vaccines.
  • Sub-Saharan Africa / tropical South America: yellow fever
  • Hajj/Umrah: meningococcal ACYW135 (mandatory)
  • Sahel meningitis belt: meningococcal
  • Malaria areas: chemoprophylaxis, not vaccine
  • Yellow fever is live: avoid in egg allergy (specialist assessment), infants under 6 months, immunosuppressed
exam_pearl: Kenya plus yellow fever option = yellow fever; meningococcal is the Hajj answer.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Same scenario as 1089 but with Yellow Fever option added; here Yellow Fever is highlighted.

stem: teenager, poor diet and sedentary lifestyle presents for evaluation. Her mother have DM Bp: 138/80 Bmi: 29 (not sure) Which of the following factors poses the highest risk to her health?
OptA: Family history of diabetes and high BMI
OptB: Sedentary lifestyle and poor dietary habits
why_right: This recall's key is the sedentary lifestyle and poor diet, because they are the underlying, modifiable drivers of her other findings (BMI 29, borderline blood pressure) and of her future diabetes and cardiovascular risk. Family history cannot be changed, and her weight and blood pressure are largely consequences of these behaviours, so addressing lifestyle gives the greatest health benefit.
why_wrong_block:
A. Family history and high BMI do raise diabetes risk, but family history is non-modifiable and the BMI is itself a downstream result of the diet and inactivity; it would be right if the question asked for the strongest risk factor for type 2 diabetes specifically.
C. BP 138/80 falls in the stage 1 hypertension range for adolescents aged 13 or older, but it is a single reading that must be repeated and is largely a consequence of weight and lifestyle; it would be the answer only if confirmed hypertension were the focus.
key_concept:
Prevention questions: target the root, modifiable behaviour.
  • Non-modifiable: age, sex, family history
  • Modifiable: diet, physical inactivity, smoking, weight
  • Lifestyle change (diet plus ≥30 min exercise most days) lowers progression to diabetes
  • Adolescent BP is interpreted with age-specific thresholds and repeat readings
exam_pearl: When asked which factor poses the most risk in a lifestyle scenario, choose the modifiable behaviour that drives the rest.

stem: 23-year-old female has a height of 157 cm and a weight of 87 kg. What is her Body Mass Index (BMI)? Height = 1.57 m Weight = 87 kg
why_right: This recall is keyed to 25 kg/m², the cut-off where overweight begins. BMI is calculated as weight (kg) ÷ height (m)², using the stem's 87 kg and 1.57 m; square the height first, then divide. Recheck this arithmetic yourself and see the answer concern on this key.
why_wrong_block:
B. 30 is the cut-off for class I obesity; at 1.57 m it corresponds to a weight of about 74 kg, less than this patient's 87 kg.
C. 35 is the cut-off for class II obesity (about 86 kg at 1.57 m); see the answer concern regarding this option.
D. 40 is the cut-off for class III obesity; at 1.57 m it corresponds to a weight of about 99 kg, more than this patient's 87 kg.
key_concept:
BMI = kg ÷ m² (square the height in metres first).
  • <18.5 underweight; 18.5 to 24.9 normal
  • 25 to 29.9 overweight
  • 30 to 34.9 obesity class I
  • 35 to 39.9 obesity class II
  • ≥40 obesity class III
exam_pearl: Forgetting to square the height (87 ÷ 1.57) or dividing by height only gives nonsense; always square metres.

stem: To gather all data from multiples researchers and put them in 1 table to form a conclusion
highlight_terms_source: gather all data from multiples researchers and put them in 1 table
key_concept:
Systematic review = organised search and appraisal of all studies; meta-analysis = statistical pooling of their results.
  • A meta-analysis is usually performed inside a systematic review.
  • Pooled numeric estimate or forest plot: meta-analysis.
  • Narrative or qualitative synthesis only: systematic review.
  • Both sit at the top of the evidence hierarchy (secondary research).
exam_pearl: Words like 'combine', 'pool' or 'statistically' point to meta-analysis; 'search', 'identify all studies' or 'appraise' without pooling points to systematic review.
compiler_note:
Compiler note: Options recalled as abbreviations only ('Sr', 'Ma', then '??'); likely systematic review vs meta-analysis. No answer marked.
⚠ The source marked no answer for this recall (page and next page checked).

stem: (Photo of recall) Cardiovascular risk chart question: This picture came again: the patient age was 72 or 74, non diabetic non smoker, cholesterol was high, can't remember exactly the risk. Other version: Male, 75 years, nondiabetic, nonsmoker, total cholesterol 6.2, hdl 1. What is the 10-year cardiovascular risk?
highlight_terms_source: Male, 75 years, nondiabetic, nonsmoker, total cholesterol 6.2, hdl 1
key_concept:
How to read a risk chart: pick the right table, then the cell.
  • Sex, then diabetes status, then smoking status selects the table.
  • Age band selects the block.
  • Systolic BP selects the row; total cholesterol (and HDL in point based tools) selects the column.
  • Read the colour band or points total as 10 year risk.
  • Age is the strongest single contributor in the elderly.
exam_pearl: Recheck the exam image for SBP and treated status; one row change in SBP can move an elderly man across a whole risk band.

Compiler note: Note on image: 'Cardiovascular risk will be calculated with the full recall.' WHO/ISH-style risk prediction charts shown.

stem: 45 year-old male smoker 20 pack per year, no symptoms, his father has lung cancer. What is the most important step regarding screening?
key_concept:
Lung cancer screening (USPSTF 2021): annual low dose CT.
  • Age 50 to 80 years.
  • At least 20 pack years.
  • Current smoker or quit within the past 15 years.
  • Stop when quit more than 15 years or limited life expectancy.
  • Smoking cessation is offered to all smokers, screened or not.
exam_pearl: Older banks used age 55 and 30 pack years; either way a 45 year old is not yet eligible, whatever his family history.

stem: A researcher wants to study the effect of Drug X. He found several published studies with small sample sizes and wants to collect and compare their results statistically to reach a more reliable conclusion. What is the most appropriate study design to use?
highlight_terms_source: several published studies with small sample sizes
collect and compare their results statistically
why_right: The researcher has 'several published studies with small sample sizes' and wants to collect and compare their results statistically to reach a more reliable conclusion. Pooling the results of existing studies into one summary estimate is the definition of a meta-analysis, which increases power and precision beyond any single small study.
why_wrong_block:
A. Cohort study: a primary study that follows exposed and unexposed people forward to compare outcome incidence; right when the aim is to measure incidence or relative risk, not to combine published studies.
B. Case–control study: a primary study that starts from people with and without the outcome and looks back at exposure (odds ratio); right for rare diseases, not for pooling existing results.
key_concept:
Primary vs secondary research.
  • Primary: cohort, case–control, cross sectional, RCT (collect new data).
  • Secondary: systematic review and meta-analysis (use published studies).
  • Meta-analysis = statistical pooling, often shown as a forest plot.
  • Main weakness: publication bias and heterogeneity between studies.
exam_pearl: 'Several published studies' plus 'combine statistically' always points to meta-analysis; without statistical pooling it would be a systematic review.

stem: In a population of 50,000 individuals during the year 2024, there were 250 new cases of diabetes and 50 deaths due to diabetes. What is the mortality rate for diabetes per 1,000 population?
why_right: Cause specific mortality rate = deaths from the disease ÷ total population × 1,000. Here 50 deaths ÷ 50,000 population × 1,000 = 1 per 1,000. The 250 new cases are a distractor; they are used for incidence, not mortality.
why_wrong_block:
A. 0.5 per 1,000: would need 25 deaths in 50,000 (or doubling the denominator); it does not fit the given numbers.
C. 5 per 1,000: this is the incidence rate (250 new cases ÷ 50,000 × 1,000), right if the question asked for new cases of diabetes.
D. 10 per 1,000: would require 500 events in 50,000; it does not correspond to any rate from this stem.
key_concept:
Know which numerator and denominator each rate uses.

OptC: Don't do anything to boost immunity

B. Eat packaged snack only: impractical and not the recommended measure; the principle is to avoid contaminated water and raw food, not to restrict the diet to packaged products.

  • Bottled, boiled or treated water; avoid ice and tap water.

stem: Sample size 500: 300 not exercise, 200 exercise. 30 out of 200 get obese, 50 out of 300 get obese. What is the odds ratio?
why_right: Take exercise as the exposure. Odds of obesity in exercisers = 30 ÷ 170 = 0.176; in non exercisers = 50 ÷ 250 = 0.2. OR = 0.176 ÷ 0.2 ≈ 0.88, and the closest option is 0.8, meaning exercise is associated with lower odds of obesity.
why_wrong_block:
A. 0.6: would require much lower odds in the exercising group than the data show; it does not result from the 2×2 table.
C. 1.2: OR above 1 would mean exercise increases the odds of obesity; a value near this only appears if the groups are inverted (non exercise as the exposure, OR ≈ 1.13).
D. 0.4: far too strong a protective effect for these numbers; it is not obtained by any correct arrangement of the table.
key_concept:
Odds ratio from a 2×2 table: OR = (a/b) ÷ (c/d) = ad/bc.
  • a = exposed with outcome (30), b = exposed without (170).
  • c = unexposed with outcome (50), d = unexposed without (250).
  • OR = (30×250) ÷ (170×50) ≈ 0.88.
  • OR < 1 protective, = 1 no association, > 1 risk factor; never negative.
  • Use 'without outcome' counts (170, 250), not group totals; that would give the relative risk (0.15 ÷ 0.167 = 0.9).
exam_pearl: Define the exposure as the factor being studied (exercise); swapping exposed and unexposed inverts the OR (0.88 becomes 1.13).

stem: 50 asthma pts in 500 child school in past 5 years, what is the term describing this?
why_right: The stem counts all children who had asthma at any time "in the past 5 years" (50) and divides by the school population (500). Counting every existing case (old and new) over a defined span of time is period prevalence (50/500 = 10% over 5 years).
why_wrong_block:
B. Point prevalence counts existing cases at a single moment (e.g. "on the day of the survey"); here the window is 5 years.
C. Incidence rate counts only NEW cases per person-time at risk; the stem does not separate new from existing cases or give person-time.
D. Cumulative incidence is new cases over a period divided by the population initially free of disease; it would need a disease-free cohort followed forward, not a count of all asthmatics.
key_concept:
Prevalence = existing cases (old + new); incidence = new cases only.
  • Point prevalence: cases at one moment / population
  • Period prevalence: cases at any time during a period / population
  • Cumulative incidence (risk): new cases / population at risk at start
  • Incidence rate: new cases / person-time at risk
  • Prevalence ≈ incidence × duration
exam_pearl: "At any time during the past X years" with no new-versus-old split = period prevalence; "new cases" = incidence.

stem: A 45-year-old woman medically free with no personal or family history of cancer. Asking about when to start colon cancer screening?
OptA: No need for screening for her case
OptB: Start now with colonoscopy every 5 years
OptC: Start at age of 50 with colonoscopy
OptD: Start now with annual fecal occult blood
highlight_terms_source: no personal or family history of cancer
why_right: She is 45, asymptomatic, with no personal or family history, so she is average risk, and average-risk colorectal cancer screening now starts at 45. An annual stool occult blood test (FOBT/FIT) is one of the accepted screening tools, so "start now with annual fecal occult blood" is the only option with both the right start age and a correct interval.
why_wrong_block:
A. Every adult from 45 to 75 is screened; average risk lowers nothing below that. No screening would be right only beyond the upper age limit or with limited life expectancy.
B. The start age is right but the interval is wrong: screening colonoscopy is every 10 years. Every 5 years applies to flexible sigmoidoscopy or CT colonography (or surveillance after polyps).
C. Age 50 is the older cut-off; current guidance starts at 45. Choose 50 only when 45 is not offered in any option.

Average-risk CRC screening: start at 45 (50 only if 45 not offered), continue to 75.
  • FOBT/FIT: every year
  • Stool DNA test: every 3 years
  • Flexible sigmoidoscopy or CT colonography: every 5 years
  • Colonoscopy: every 10 years
  • Any positive stool test → colonoscopy
  • First-degree relative with CRC: start at 40 or 10 years before the youngest case
exam_pearl: Check the interval, not just the start age: colonoscopy every 5 years is a trap; it is every 10.

stem: A study included children who watch TV and children who do not, and compared their school performance. What type of study is this?

Name the design by its starting point:

  • Start with outcome (cases vs controls), look back at exposure → case-control
  • Exposure and outcome measured at one time → cross-sectional
  • Investigator assigns exposure at random → RCT
  • Groups defined by exposure + no assignment = observational

stem: During school health screening primary health doctor referred student to another doctor for eye glass as he has refractory error, what level of prevention is this.
why_right: School health screening picked up a refractive error that already existed but had not been recognised, and the student was referred for glasses. Detecting an established condition early (screening) and treating it promptly to stop it affecting learning and vision is secondary prevention.
why_wrong_block:
A. Primary prevention stops a disease from occurring at all (immunisation, health education, eye protection); the refractive error is already present here.
C. Tertiary prevention limits disability or complications of established, symptomatic disease (rehabilitation, low-vision aids for permanent loss); here the problem was found by screening and simply corrected.
key_concept:
Levels of prevention:
  • Primordial: prevent risk factors arising (healthy environment, policy)
  • Primary: prevent disease onset (vaccines, education)
  • Secondary: early detection and prompt treatment (screening programmes)
  • Tertiary: reduce disability from established disease (rehabilitation)
  • Quaternary: protect from overmedicalisation
exam_pearl: Any "screening" scenario that finds an existing silent condition = secondary, even if the fix (glasses) sounds like treatment.

stem: There is a spread of infection among the residents. Out of 200 residents, 40 show symptoms. What is the definition of a cumulative prevalence?
why_right: Prevalence is the proportion of the whole population that has the condition: 40 symptomatic / 200 residents = 0.20 = 20%. The denominator is everyone in the population (200), and the numerator is everyone who has the condition (40).
why_wrong_block:
A. 15% would be 30/200; no figure in the stem gives 30 cases.
C. 25% comes from the classic error of dividing cases by the people WITHOUT symptoms (40/160); the denominator must be the total population.
D. 10% would be 20/200, half the stated cases; it does not match the counts given.
key_concept:
Prevalence = people with the condition / total population at that time.
  • Here: 40 / 200 = 20%
  • Denominator = everyone (cases + non-cases)
  • Cases / non-cases is the odds, not a proportion
  • Incidence needs NEW cases among those initially at risk
exam_pearl: If an answer equals cases divided by non-cases (40/160 = 25%), that is the odds trap.

stem: Researchers want to see the relation between pediatric groups and obesity. They mentioned a lot of objectives for the research and multiple criteria to diagnose, more than 3. What is the best test for IBP strategy?
highlight_terms_source: multiple criteria to diagnose, more than 3
why_right: The outcome (obesity status) is being classified by multiple criteria into more than 3 categories, so the dependent variable is categorical with more than two unordered levels. The regression built for that is multinomial (polytomous) logistic regression, which also handles several predictors such as pediatric age groups.
why_wrong_block:
A. A t test compares the MEAN of a continuous variable between exactly two groups; it cannot model a multi-category outcome or several predictors.
B. Linear regression needs a CONTINUOUS outcome (e.g. BMI value or weight in kg), not obesity categories.
C. Standard (binary) logistic regression fits an outcome with only TWO categories (obese vs not obese); it becomes the right answer if obesity is a yes/no outcome.
key_concept:
Choose the test by the outcome variable:
  • Continuous outcome, 2 groups → t test; ≥3 groups → ANOVA
  • Continuous outcome with predictors → linear regression
  • Binary outcome → logistic regression
  • Categorical outcome with >2 unordered levels → multinomial logistic regression
  • Ordered categories → ordinal logistic regression
  • Two categorical variables in a table → chi-square
exam_pearl: Binary outcome = logistic; more than two outcome categories = multinomial. Count the outcome categories first.

stem: 47 years old Female came to preventive clinic, no family history, medical history positive for HTN for 5 years, BMI 37 what is the appropriate screening test:
why_right: The decisive clues are BMI 37 (obesity) and hypertension for 5 years in a 47-year-old: overweight or obese adults with an extra cardiometabolic risk factor (and all adults from 35 to 70 who are overweight) should be screened for type 2 diabetes. Fasting blood glucose is a standard screening test (diabetes ≥ 7.0 mmol/L, prediabetes 5.6 to 6.9), so it is the screening most directly driven by her risk profile.
why_wrong_block:
A. Stool occult blood is age-based colorectal screening (from 45); it is not the test her risk factors (obesity, hypertension) point to, which is what this stem is built around.
C. Pap smear is routine cervical screening for women 21 to 65 who are or have been sexually active; the stem gives no cervical risk clues, and the companion version that adds "sexually active" is keyed to Pap smear instead.
D. Lung cancer screening (low-dose CT) is for adults 50 to 80 with a heavy smoking history; no smoking history is given and she is under 50.

Screen for type 2 diabetes when an adult is overweight/obese plus a risk factor (HTN, dyslipidaemia, family history, PCOS, CVD), or overweight aged 35 to 70.
  • FBG: normal < 5.6, prediabetes 5.6 to 6.9, DM ≥ 7.0 mmol/L
  • HbA1c ≥ 6.5% = DM; 5.7 to 6.4% = prediabetes
  • 2-h OGTT ≥ 11.1 mmol/L = DM
  • Random glucose ≥ 11.1 counts only with symptoms (not a screening test)
  • Normal result → repeat at least every 3 years
exam_pearl: Obesity + hypertension in the stem = screen for diabetes; "sexually active" in the stem shifts the key to Pap smear.

stem: A 30-year-old man is planning to travel to a rural area in sub-Saharan Africa for 2 weeks. The area is endemic for malaria. He asks about the best preventive measure before traveling. Which of the following is the most appropriate advice?

OptB: Give yellow fever vaccine and antimalarial chemoprophylaxis

  • Doxycycline or mefloquine are alternatives
  • Chloroquine: avoided in falciparum areas (widespread resistance)
  • No malaria vaccine is recommended for travellers
  • Sub-Saharan Africa: also check yellow fever vaccination
  • Fever after return from Africa = malaria until proven otherwise
exam_pearl: A short trip does not remove the need for chemoprophylaxis in an endemic area; repellent is added to it, never a substitute.

stem: The government did a health campaign to encourage the consumption of low fat products and a low salt intake in order to decrease risk factors of hypertension and diabetes. What is the type of prevention?
why_right: The campaign targets the whole population to stop risk factors (high fat and high salt diets) from becoming established, "in order to decrease risk factors of hypertension and diabetes". Acting on the social and lifestyle conditions that create risk factors, before those risk factors exist in individuals, is primordial prevention.
why_wrong_block:
B. Primary prevention prevents the disease itself in people already exposed to a risk factor (e.g. vaccination, treating raised cholesterol, stopping smoking); here the target is the risk factors, not the diseases.
C. Secondary prevention is early detection and prompt treatment of existing, often asymptomatic disease (e.g. BP or glucose screening); no screening is involved here.
D. Tertiary prevention limits disability and complications in established disease (e.g. cardiac rehabilitation, diabetic foot care); the campaign targets healthy people.
key_concept:
Level of prevention is decided by what the intervention targets.
  • Primordial: prevent risk factors from arising (population diet, salt, smoke-free policies)
  • Primary: prevent disease onset in exposed people (vaccines, statins for high risk)
  • Secondary: screen and treat early (mammography, BP screening)
  • Tertiary: reduce complications and disability (rehabilitation)
  • Quaternary: protect patients from overmedicalisation
exam_pearl: Wording "reduce risk factors" or population lifestyle policy = primordial; "prevent the disease" in at-risk people = primary.

stem: 72 yrs old male, retired, free medical hx, experiences imbalance and falls, hx of osteoarthritis in his knee; he wants to prevent fall and strengthen his muscle. Advise him which type of exercise?
OptB: Low impact exercises like walking and aerobic water exercise
OptC: High impact exercises like jumping and running
why_right: A 72 year old with "imbalance and falls" and knee osteoarthritis needs exercise that builds strength, endurance and balance without loading the damaged joint. Low impact activity such as walking and water aerobics does this: water supports body weight, so the knee is spared while muscles are trained. It is safe, sustainable and reduces fall risk.

A. Static stretching improves flexibility only; it does not build the strength or balance he needs to prevent falls.
C. Jumping and running place high impact load on an osteoarthritic knee and raise the risk of falls and fractures in an elderly man with poor balance.
D. Discouraging exercise leads to deconditioning, muscle weakness and more falls; inactivity worsens both OA symptoms and fall risk.
key_concept:
Elderly faller with OA: low impact, strength and balance exercise.
  • Walking, swimming, water aerobics, cycling: low joint load
  • Add quadriceps strengthening and balance training (e.g. tai chi)
  • Avoid high impact running and jumping
  • Weight loss also reduces knee OA load
  • Exercise is first line treatment for knee OA, not something to avoid
exam_pearl: Rest is never the answer for OA or falls prevention; choose the joint sparing (low impact, water based) option.

stem: There was a question about MVA: patient had multiple fractures and underwent surgery but they can't control the bleeding and the patient died. They ask what is the primary cause of death.
why_right: This recall's key is bleeding: the patient died because surgeons "can't control the bleeding", so uncontrolled hemorrhage leading to hemorrhagic shock is the disease process that killed him. The fractures started the chain, but they are an injury rather than the lethal process, and cardiac arrest is only the final event. Another version of this recall is also keyed to severe bleeding; if the road traffic accident itself appears as an option, choose it.
why_wrong_block:
A. Multiple fractures are the injury that began the sequence; on their own they did not kill him, the uncontrolled bleeding did (choose the RTA or the injury only if the question asks for the underlying external cause).
C. Cardiac arrest is the mode of dying, present in every death, and is never written as a cause of death.
key_concept:
Chain of events: RTA, then multiple fractures with severe bleeding, then hemorrhagic shock, then cardiac arrest and death.
  • Immediate cause: the final disease process (hemorrhagic shock)
  • Underlying cause (WHO): the injury or external event that started the chain (RTA)
  • Mode of dying (cardiac arrest, respiratory arrest): never a cause
  • If RTA is an option, choose it
exam_pearl: Never choose cardiac or respiratory arrest as a cause of death; it is how everyone dies.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Screenshot version (RTA, multiple fractures and severe bleeding, transfused in OR but arrested and died): Answer: C (the severe bleeding). If RTA was given as an option, go for it. Sequence: RTA -> multiple fractures and severe bleeding -> hemorrhagic shock -> cardiac arrest -> death. Multiple fractures per se is a diagnosis rather than a cause; severe bleeding is the primary underlying cause.

stem: TB test in a city: they had 200 cases beginning of the year, now 50 new cases, 20 died. What is the incidence rate per 1000?
why_right: Incidence counts only new cases arising during the period: here "50 new cases". The 200 cases present at the start of the year are prevalent cases and the 20 deaths are mortality, so both are distractors. The population size was not kept in the recall; the key of 5 per 1000 corresponds to 50 new cases in a population of 10,000 (50 / 10,000 x 1000 = 5).
why_wrong_block:
A. 2 per 1000 is what the 20 deaths give over 10,000 people: that is the mortality rate, not incidence.
C. 20 per 1000 comes from the 200 existing cases over 10,000: that is prevalence at the start of the year, not incidence.
D. 50 is the raw number of new cases, not a rate per 1000 population.
key_concept:
Incidence = new cases during the period / population at risk x 1000.
  • Use only new cases in the numerator
  • Existing cases at the start belong to prevalence (and are not at risk)
  • Deaths / population = mortality rate
  • Deaths / cases = case fatality rate
  • Prevalence = existing cases (old + new) / population
exam_pearl: Old cases and deaths in an incidence question are traps; only new cases go on top.

stem: Ministry of health in x country is detecting flu cases in the winter season, they gather data from hospitals, health centers, labs. What is the type of surveillance?
OptA: Sentinel surveillance from selected reporting sites
highlight_terms_source: flu cases in the winter season
gather data from hospitals, health centers, labs
why_right: Seasonal influenza is classically monitored through sentinel surveillance: a chosen network of hospitals, health centres and laboratories reports influenza like illness and sends samples during the season. Data from designated reporting sites for "flu cases in the winter season" is the sentinel model, giving trends and circulating strains without needing reports from every facility.
why_wrong_block:
B. Active surveillance means health authorities go out and actively search for cases (visits, calls, record review), as in outbreak investigation or polio eradication; the stem describes facilities reporting data.
C. Passive surveillance is routine notification by all providers on their own initiative, as with notifiable diseases; it is right when the stem describes all facilities reporting without selection.
D. Syndromic surveillance tracks symptom patterns or indirect data (ED complaints, drug sales, absenteeism) before diagnosis is confirmed; laboratory confirmed flu cases are not syndromic data.
key_concept:
Match the surveillance type to who collects and from where.
  • Sentinel: selected sites report, e.g. influenza
  • Passive: all providers report routinely (notifiable diseases); cheap, underreports
  • Active: authority seeks cases (outbreaks, eradication)
  • Syndromic: symptom or proxy data before diagnosis
exam_pearl: Influenza season monitoring = sentinel; "health department visits or calls to find cases" = active.

stem: 200 people randomly assigned Half will take vaccine Half will take placebo Will be monitored over 1 year Type of study?
why_right: Participants were "randomly assigned" by the investigators to vaccine or placebo and then followed forward for 1 year. Investigator assigned exposure with randomisation and a placebo control defines a randomized clinical trial, the strongest single design for testing an intervention.
why_wrong_block:
A. A cohort also follows people forward, but the exposure is observed, not assigned by the researcher; random allocation makes this experimental.
B. Case control starts with people who have the outcome and controls without it, then looks back at exposures; nothing is assigned here.
C. Cross sectional measures exposure and outcome at one point in time; this study has follow up over a year.
key_concept:
Ask first: did the investigator assign the exposure?
  • Yes, randomly: RCT (experimental)
  • No, follow exposed vs unexposed forward: cohort
  • No, start from outcome and look back: case control
  • No, single time point: cross sectional
exam_pearl: "Randomly assigned" or "placebo" in the stem means trial, even though people are followed over time like a cohort.

stem: Researchers make New drug best way to measure effectiveness (this My word i dont remmber the exact word of the stem)
why_right: To measure whether a new drug works, the best design is a randomized controlled trial: random allocation balances known and unknown confounders, so the difference in outcome can be attributed to the drug. A new drug has no prior trials, so primary experimental evidence must come from an RCT.
why_wrong_block:
A. A cohort is observational; patients who choose or are prescribed the drug differ from those who are not, so confounding limits conclusions about effectiveness. It suits harms or long term outcomes after approval.
C. Meta analysis sits higher in the evidence hierarchy but pools existing trials; it cannot be done for a new drug with no trials yet.
key_concept:
Best design depends on the question.
  • Effect of a new treatment: RCT
  • Summarising many existing RCTs: systematic review and meta analysis
  • Rare disease cause: case control
  • Incidence, prognosis, rare exposure: cohort
  • Prevalence: cross sectional
exam_pearl: Meta analysis beats a single RCT only when there are already several trials to pool.

stem: Cholera outbreak and the Dr wants to see the daily cases and the variation: 12, 15, 8, 16, 9, 3, 12. What is the central tendency measurement?

Central tendency = mean, median, mode; dispersion = range, variance, SD, IQR.

  • Skewed or outlier present: median
  • Categorical / most frequent: mode
  • Spread of data: range (crude), SD (with mean), IQR (with median)
  • Here: mean ≈ 10.7, median 12, mode 12, range 13

stem: 23-year-old male recently arrived from Sudan presented with fever and jaundice, blood film confirmed the presence of malaria, which mosquito type is known to transfer the disease to human?
why_right: Malaria ("recently arrived from Sudan", fever, jaundice from hemolysis, positive blood film) is transmitted by the bite of the female Anopheles mosquito, which needs a blood meal to develop her eggs and injects sporozoites with her saliva. Males feed on plant juices and do not transmit disease. In Sudan the usual species is Plasmodium falciparum.
why_wrong_block:
B. Aedes aegypti is the main vector of dengue, yellow fever, chikungunya and Zika (day biter, peak early morning); choose it when the traveller has retro-orbital pain, "breakbone" myalgia or hemorrhagic features.
C. Culex pipiens transmits West Nile virus and lymphatic filariasis, not Plasmodium.
D. Aedes albopictus (tiger mosquito) is a secondary vector of dengue and chikungunya, not malaria.
key_concept:
Match the mosquito to the disease.
  • Female Anopheles: malaria
  • Aedes aegypti: dengue, yellow fever, chikungunya, Zika
  • Aedes albopictus: dengue, chikungunya
  • Culex: West Nile virus, lymphatic filariasis
  • Malaria diagnosis: thick and thin blood smear, repeat if negative
exam_pearl: Only the FEMALE mosquito bites; if "Anopheles" appears without "female" it is still the malaria vector, but Aedes is the dengue trap.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Original recall: "Study about malaria, what is the mosquito targeted. Answer: female Anopheles mosquito"; compiler added the fuller "Q:" version.

stem: 40 y old women multiple sex partners came to the outpatient infection clinic. Ask about the most effective preventable method

  • Mutual monogamy with an uninfected partner: next most effective, cuts exposures
  • Consistent, correct condom use: best protection per sexual act
  • Vaccination (HBV, HPV): specific primary prevention
  • Screening and partner treatment: secondary prevention

stem: Saudi something want to inform WHO and some international organization to assess health in Saudi arabia: what is the most important variable to inform about:
why_right: To "assess health in Saudi Arabia" for the WHO, a country reports health indicators: standardised measures that summarise the health status of a population or the performance of its health system (e.g. life expectancy, infant and maternal mortality, disease incidence). They allow comparison between countries and over time, which is exactly what international bodies need.

A. Risk factors are exposures that raise the probability of disease (smoking, obesity); they explain causes but do not summarise the population's health status. Choose them when the question is about prevention targets or aetiology.
B. Confounders are a study-design concept (a third variable distorting an exposure–outcome association); they matter in analysing research, not in reporting national health status.
key_concept:
Health indicator = measurable summary of population health or health-system performance.

  • Morbidity: incidence, prevalence
  • Summary: life expectancy, DALYs
  • Service: vaccine coverage, skilled birth attendance
  • Determinant / risk factor = cause; indicator = measured status

stem: 15 years worker in chemical factory want to screen for cancer, what is the most sensitive test?
why_right: This recall's key is the Ames test, the classic short-term screening test for the mutagenic (and so possibly carcinogenic) potential of a chemical. It uses histidine-dependent Salmonella strains: a chemical that causes mutations lets the bacteria revert and grow on histidine-free medium, often with liver enzyme (S9) activation added. It is quick, cheap and the first-line test in carcinogen screening batteries, which is why exam recalls key it as the "most sensitive" screen.
why_wrong_block:
A. Cell transformation assays look for malignant-like change in cultured mammalian cells; they are slower and more labour-intensive and are used as follow-up rather than first-line screening.
C. Unscheduled DNA synthesis measures DNA repair activity (usually in hepatocytes) after exposure; it is a second-tier confirmatory genotoxicity test, not the main screen.
D. Cytogenetic tests (chromosomal aberrations, micronuclei, sister chromatid exchange) detect chromosome damage; in exposed workers they are used for biological monitoring of peripheral lymphocytes rather than for screening the chemical.
key_concept:
Short-term tests for chemical carcinogens/mutagens.
  • Ames (bacterial reverse mutation): first-line, rapid, cheap screen of the chemical
  • Mammalian cell mutation and cell transformation assays: follow-up
  • Unscheduled DNA synthesis: DNA repair, confirmatory
  • Cytogenetics (aberrations, micronucleus, SCE): chromosome damage; biomonitoring of exposed workers
exam_pearl: These tests assess the CHEMICAL; a test on the worker's own cells would be cytogenetic biomonitoring.

stem: A 40-year-old P5005 woman presented to the Clinic. She has a strong family history of cancer where both her mother and sister died of cancer. BMI 31 kg/m2 Which of the following is the most appropriate counselling?
OptD: Meet nutritional needs through diet alone
why_right: The decisive clue is "BMI 31 kg/m2": she is obese, and excess body weight is the key modifiable risk factor for several cancers (endometrial, postmenopausal breast, colorectal). With a strong family history of cancer, the most targeted counselling is to reach and maintain a healthy weight; the other options are general lifestyle advice that serve this goal.
why_wrong_block:
A. Physical activity is good advice for everyone, but here it is a means to the more specific goal of weight control; it would be the answer if her BMI were normal and she were sedentary.
C. Limiting fast food is generic dietary advice that does not directly name her main modifiable risk factor, obesity.
D. Meeting nutrition through diet rather than supplements is a general cancer-prevention message, not targeted to her raised BMI.
key_concept:
Cancer prevention counselling targets the abnormal modifiable factor in the stem.
  • High BMI: maintain a healthy weight
  • Smoker: stop smoking
  • Sedentary, normal weight: physical activity
  • Family history: also consider earlier or enhanced screening
exam_pearl: When the stem gives an abnormal BMI, the counselling answer is healthy weight, not exercise.

stem: The patient was a smoker for 20 years I believe
OptB: Advice him to quit smoking (like only quit smoking is enough)
why_right: Per USPSTF, a smoker who meets both criteria, age 50 to 80 years and at least 20 pack-years (current smoker or quit within the last 15 years), should have annual low-dose CT lung cancer screening. This recall's key assumes he qualifies: "a smoker for 20 years" at about a pack a day gives roughly 20 pack-years, and his age is taken to be 50 or older. Screening is then added to cessation advice, not replaced by it.
why_wrong_block: B. Smoking cessation advice is always given, but on its own it is not enough for an eligible patient; it would be the only answer if he did not meet the criteria (e.g. aged 49, or under 20 pack-years, or quit more than 15 years ago).
key_concept:
USPSTF lung cancer screening: annual low-dose CT.
  • Age 50 to 80 years
  • ≥20 pack-years
  • Current smoker or quit within 15 years
  • Stop once quit for 15 years or limited life expectancy
  • Chest X-ray and sputum cytology are NOT screening tests
exam_pearl: Check age AND pack-years: 20 pack-years at age 49 means no screening yet, only cessation.

stem: A 60 yr old man went to family med clinic for regular checkups. He's asking if there's any vaccine he can take:
why_right: A healthy 60-year-old at a routine check-up qualifies for pneumococcal vaccination, since current CDC advice gives it to all adults from age 50 (older guidance used age 65). It protects against invasive pneumococcal disease and pneumonia, which rise with age; influenza, zoster and a Td/Tdap booster are the other age-appropriate vaccines.
why_wrong_block:
A. MMR is live and given to adults only when they lack evidence of immunity (e.g. non-immune women before pregnancy, health workers); it is not routine for a 60-year-old.
C. Meningococcal vaccine is not routine in adults; it is for specific risks such as asplenia, complement deficiency, Hajj/Umrah travel or outbreaks.
D. DTaP is the paediatric formulation (under 7 years); adults receive Tdap once and then Td or Tdap boosters every 10 years.
key_concept:
Routine vaccines for an older adult.
  • Pneumococcal: all adults ≥50 (current CDC), plus younger adults with risk conditions
  • Influenza: yearly
  • Recombinant zoster: ≥50
  • Td/Tdap booster every 10 years
  • Meningococcal, MMR: only for specific indications
exam_pearl: Capital letters matter: DTaP is for children; adults get Tdap/Td.

stem: Woman heavy smoker, will start on exercise program and she doesn't know the risk on health , what type of model?
highlight_terms_source: doesn't know the risk on health
why_right: The decisive clue is that she "doesn't know the risk on health": the gap is in her perception of the threat, not in her readiness or skills. The Health belief model predicts that a person acts on a health behaviour (quitting, exercising) once she perceives herself as susceptible to a serious threat and believes the benefits outweigh the barriers. Education here aims to raise perceived susceptibility and severity, which is exactly what this model targets.
why_wrong_block:
B. Health promotion model (Pender) focuses on building positive health behaviours through personal factors, self efficacy and situational influences, not on making the person aware of a specific threat; it fits a wellness or lifestyle enhancement framing rather than "she doesn't know the risk".
C. The transtheoretical model classifies readiness to change into stages (precontemplation to maintenance); it would be right if the stem asked which stage she is in or described her intention to quit, not her lack of risk knowledge.
key_concept:
Match the model to what the stem says is missing.
  • Lacks knowledge or perception of risk: Health belief model
  • Stage of readiness to change (precontemplation, contemplation, preparation, action, maintenance): Transtheoretical model
  • Behaviour driven by attitudes plus what important others think: Theory of reasoned action
  • Spread of a new idea or practice through a community: Diffusion of innovation
  • Enhancing wellness through self efficacy and perceived benefits: Health promotion model
exam_pearl: "Doesn't know the risk" or "perceived susceptibility/severity" = Health belief model; "ready/planning/already started" = transtheoretical stages.

stem: A woman with no background of hypertension (HTN) has been diagnosed with it. What is the best way to educate her about the risk factors?
why_right: She is newly diagnosed and the task is to educate her about the risk factors, so the aim is to change how she perceives the threat. The Health belief model states that people take preventive action when they see the threat as serious and themselves as personally susceptible, and when benefits of action outweigh barriers. Risk factor education directly targets these perceptions.
why_wrong_block:
A. The health promotion model centres on self efficacy and enhancing overall wellness behaviours; it is less specific to communicating the seriousness and personal relevance of a disease risk.
C. Theory of reasoned action explains behaviour through intention, shaped by personal attitudes and subjective norms (what important others expect); it fits a stem about family or social pressure, not risk education.
D. Diffusion of innovation describes how a new idea or technology spreads through a population (innovators, early adopters, majority, laggards); it applies to community uptake of a new programme, not one patient's counselling.
key_concept:
Health belief model components: perceived susceptibility, perceived severity, perceived benefits, perceived barriers, cues to action, self efficacy.
  • Risk education for an individual: Health belief model
  • Attitudes plus social norms drive intention: Theory of reasoned action
  • Population adoption of something new: Diffusion of innovation
  • Readiness stages: Transtheoretical model
exam_pearl: Whenever the stem stresses making the patient understand how serious or likely the risk is, choose the Health belief model.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Embedded screenshot (Q139) under 2213: Answer B, The Health Belief Model proposes that people are most likely to take preventative action if they perceive the threat of a health risk to be serious and if they feel they are personally susceptible.

stem: Biostat question asking to calculate the rate of people affected 30 kids with gastroenteritis 150 people total
why_right: The proportion affected is cases divided by the population at risk: 30 / 150 = 0.20 = 20%. In an outbreak this proportion is the attack rate (a cumulative incidence), so the numerator is the 30 children with gastroenteritis and the denominator is all 150 people exposed.
why_wrong_block:
A. 10% would require 15 cases out of 150; it does not match the given numbers.
B. 15% would require about 22 cases out of 150; a common slip is dividing by the wrong denominator.
D. 25% would come from 30 / 120, i.e. using only the unaffected people as the denominator; the denominator must be the whole population at risk (150).
key_concept:
Attack rate = new cases during the outbreak / population at risk at the start, × 100.
  • Denominator = everyone exposed (affected + unaffected)
  • Secondary attack rate = cases among contacts / total susceptible contacts
  • Prevalence uses existing cases at a point in time; incidence uses new cases over a period
exam_pearl: Do not divide cases by non-cases (that gives odds, 30/120 = 25%), divide by the total at risk.

stem: If you had to raise awareness to the public which one would u choose (worded better than that)
why_right: A public awareness or national screening programme should be built on priority and impact: a common cancer with a long detectable precancerous phase and an effective, acceptable screening test. Colorectal cancer is among the most common cancers in Saudi Arabia and is screenable in average risk adults (colonoscopy, stool tests), with polyp removal preventing cancer, so it gives the greatest population benefit.
why_wrong_block:
A. Oral cancer is relatively uncommon in the general population and population screening is not recommended; targeted awareness fits high risk groups (tobacco, shamma or betel users) rather than the whole public.
B. Pancreatic cancer has no effective screening test for average risk people and is usually detected late; screening is reserved for selected high risk hereditary syndromes, so a public campaign would have little impact.
key_concept:
Choose the screening target by burden + test availability + treatable early stage.
  • Colorectal: average risk screening from 45 (choose 50 if 45 is not offered); colonoscopy every 10 years or annual stool test
  • Lung: only for heavy smokers, not the general public
  • Pancreatic and oral: no average risk population screening
exam_pearl: If lung appears as an option, remember it is screened only in heavy smokers, while colorectal applies to everyone above the start age, which is why colorectal wins for a general public programme.

A) Lung B) Colorectal C) Pancreatic D) Oral cancer' Answer: B (pen tick): Colorectal cancer is amongst the most common cancers in KSA; lung cancer screening is typically for smokers whereas colon cancer screening is for anyone above 50.
