stem: WHO report that the Case-fatality is 37.4% for Mers Cov, what does the percentage means?
OptA: Number of population at risk for Mers Cov infection
OptB: Number of Infant who will catch the infection if their mother is +ve
OptC: Number of death among infected people with Mers Cov
OptD: Number of people diagnosed with Mers Cov
why_right: Case fatality rate = number of deaths from the disease / number of people diagnosed with that disease, × 100. A CFR of 37.4% for MERS CoV therefore means that about 37 of every 100 infected (confirmed) cases died. It measures disease severity (lethality), not how common the infection is.
why_wrong_block:
A. The population at risk is the denominator for incidence or attack rate, not the CFR; CFR only counts people who already have the disease.
B. Infants infected by a positive mother describes the vertical transmission rate, an unrelated measure.
D. The number of people diagnosed is the denominator of the CFR (or a case count for incidence/prevalence); the percentage refers to deaths among them, not the diagnoses themselves.
key_concept:
Mortality measures differ by denominator.
  • Case fatality rate: deaths from disease / cases of that disease (severity)
  • Cause specific mortality rate: deaths from disease / total population
  • Crude mortality rate: all deaths / total population
  • Attack rate: new cases / population at risk
exam_pearl: CFR denominator is the sick, mortality rate denominator is the whole population.

stem: Long case about Researcher investigates food poisoning after a trip, he does interviews and identifies what food caused it.
OptA: case control to comber between affected and health
why_right: The researcher starts from the outcome (people who got food poisoning) and interviews them and unaffected people about past exposures (what they ate) to find the culprit food. Starting from disease status and looking back at exposures is the definition of a case control study, which is quick, cheap and suited to identifying the source in an outbreak.
why_wrong_block:
B. A cohort study starts from exposure status and follows groups to compare who develops the outcome; it fits when you define eaters versus non eaters of a specific food first, not when you compare affected with healthy people to find an unknown cause.
C. A randomized controlled trial assigns an intervention prospectively; it would be unethical and impossible to randomize people to contaminated food, and it is used to test treatments, not investigate outbreaks.
key_concept:
Identify the design by the starting point.
  • Start with disease, look back at exposure: case control (gives odds ratio)
  • Start with exposure, follow to outcome: cohort (gives relative risk, incidence)
  • Investigator assigns exposure randomly: RCT
  • Exposure and outcome at one time point: cross sectional (prevalence)
exam_pearl: If the stem lists everyone on the trip and computes food specific attack rates by what each person ate, that is a retrospective cohort; if it compares ill versus well people, choose case control.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Screenshot (item 7), 'case control' highlighted, Answer: A.

stem: A 50-year-old man with a history of heavy smoking presents for a routine health checkup. He is asymptomatic and has no known chronic medical conditions. According to preventive screening recommendations, which of the following conditions is most important to screen for in this patient?
why_right: He is 50, asymptomatic and average risk for colorectal cancer, so he is within the age band for routine colorectal cancer screening (starts at 45, or 50 if 45 is not offered), using colonoscopy every 10 years or a stool based test. Among the options, it is the only screening recommended for all adults at his age.
why_wrong_block:
A. Osteoporosis screening (DEXA) is routine for women aged 65 and older or younger postmenopausal women with risk factors; it is not recommended for a 50 year old man without risk factors.
C. One time ultrasound screening for abdominal aortic aneurysm is for men aged 65 to 75 who have ever smoked; his smoking history matters, but at 50 he is too young.
D. Prostate cancer screening with PSA is not routine; it is an individual shared decision, typically discussed from 55 to 69, so it is not the most important screen here.
key_concept:
Screening by age in an average risk adult man.
  • Colorectal: from 45 (50 if 45 not listed)
  • Lung (LDCT): age 50 to 80 with heavy pack year history
  • AAA (ultrasound once): men 65 to 75 who ever smoked
  • PSA: shared decision, 55 to 69
  • Osteoporosis: women ≥65
exam_pearl: "Heavy smoker" tempts you to AAA, but AAA screening starts at 65; if low dose CT for lung cancer were offered, it would compete strongly at 50.

stem: Female 42 wants cancer screening, smoker for 18 years, no family history of cancer:
why_right: She is a 42 year old woman with no family history, so she is average risk and falls within the Saudi MOH breast screening window (women aged 40 to 50, mammogram every 2 years). Bilateral mammogram is therefore the screening test due now; her smoking history does not yet qualify her for other cancer screens.
why_wrong_block:
B. Colorectal cancer screening in average risk adults starts at 45; at 42 with no family history she is not yet eligible.
C. Lung cancer screening with low dose CT is for adults aged 50 to 80 with a heavy pack year history; at 42 she is too young despite 18 years of smoking.
D. All of the above is wrong because only breast screening is indicated at her age; colon and lung screening are not yet due.
key_concept:
Age gates decide which screen is due.
  • Breast (MOH): mammogram every 2 years, women 40 to 50
  • Colorectal: from 45 (average risk)
  • Lung: LDCT from 50 in heavy smokers
  • Cervical: Pap smear for sexually active women in the recommended age band
exam_pearl: Smoking is a distractor here: it does not lower the lung screening start age below 50, so the age decides the answer.

stem: 40-year-old patient diagnosed with essential HTN, the doctor discussed with him the role of physical activity in reducing cardiovascular risk. Which of the following is the recommended physical activity?
OptC: 30 min brisk walking for 5 times a week
OptD: 10 min cycling most days of the week
why_right: For cardiovascular risk reduction in essential hypertension, adults should do at least 150 minutes per week of moderate intensity aerobic exercise, spread over most days. 30 minutes of brisk walking 5 times a week equals exactly 150 minutes of moderate aerobic activity, which lowers blood pressure and cardiovascular risk.
why_wrong_block:
A. 10 minutes of swimming once a week totals only 10 minutes, far below the 150 minutes per week target, and once weekly lacks the regular frequency needed.
B. Weight lifting every 2 weeks is too infrequent and resistance training is an adjunct, not a replacement, for regular aerobic exercise in hypertension.
D. 10 minutes of cycling most days gives roughly 50 to 70 minutes per week, still well short of the 150 minute target.
key_concept:
Exercise prescription for CV risk: ≥150 min/week moderate aerobic activity.
  • Typical form: 30 min on 5 days per week (brisk walking, cycling, swimming)
  • Spread over at least 3 days per week, with no more than 2 consecutive days off
  • Resistance training: an add on, not a substitute
exam_pearl: Multiply minutes by frequency; only the option reaching about 150 minutes per week of aerobic activity is correct.

stem: A patient presents to the clinic seeking help with smoking cessation. He already bought nicotine replacement and he has desire to stop? What this stage called:
why_right: This recall's key is Action, reasoning that buying nicotine replacement and coming to the clinic for cessation help are concrete steps beyond merely thinking about quitting. However, in the transtheoretical model, Action means the person has already changed the behaviour (has stopped smoking, within the last 6 months). A smoker who "has desire to stop" and has bought NRT but not yet quit is classically in Preparation (intends to act soon and has taken small steps). Review this card against your source.
why_wrong_block:
A. Preparation: intends to quit in the near future and has taken preparatory steps such as buying NRT, setting a quit date or seeking help; this description fits the stem closely, which is why the card is flagged.
C. Contemplation: aware of the problem and thinking about quitting within the next 6 months but has taken no concrete steps; here he has already bought NRT.
D. Precontemplation: no intention to change in the foreseeable future, often unaware or denying the problem; he actively wants to stop, so this does not fit.
key_concept:
Transtheoretical (stages of change) model.
  • Precontemplation: not considering change
  • Contemplation: thinking about change, no steps yet
  • Preparation: planning soon, small steps taken (bought NRT, set date)
  • Action: behaviour actually changed, less than 6 months
  • Maintenance: change sustained beyond 6 months
exam_pearl: Bought the tools but still smoking = Preparation; has actually stopped = Action.
compiler_note: Repeats: appears 2× in this file (also AS-2470).

stem: A patient has recently stopped smoking and has started using nicotine replacement patches. The patient is motivated to quit smoking and is actively taking steps towards achieving that goal. Which stage of smoking cessation is the patient currently in?
why_right: The patient has "recently stopped smoking" and is "actively taking steps" (already on nicotine patches). The behaviour itself has changed, and only recently, which defines the Action stage. Action covers roughly the first 6 months after the change; after that it becomes maintenance.
why_wrong_block:
B. Preparation is intending to quit within the next month with a plan (e.g. setting a quit date, buying patches) but not yet stopped. Here he has already stopped.
C. Contemplation is recognising smoking is harmful and thinking of quitting in the coming months without concrete steps. This patient has moved well past thinking.
D. Precontemplation is no intention to quit and often no recognition of the problem. Right for a smoker who sees no reason to stop.
key_concept:
Stages of change (Prochaska): match the stage to intention and behaviour, not to how motivated the patient sounds.
  • Precontemplation: no intention to change in the next 6 months; unaware of or denies the problem
  • Contemplation: aware of the problem, intends to change within about 6 months, no concrete steps
  • Preparation: intends to act within the next month and has made a plan or small steps
  • Action: has actually changed the behaviour within the last 6 months
  • Maintenance: change sustained beyond 6 months
  • Relapse can occur at any point and returns the patient to an earlier stage
exam_pearl: Already quit (even with NRT help) and less than 6 months = Action; planning with a date in the next month = Preparation.

stem: A question about a patient who visited a clinic, for some reason the doctor advised him to do surgery, the patient was afraid to do the surgery. He does not know the complications if he does not do the surgery. Which stage of change is this ?
why_right: The patient is advised surgery but "does not know the complications if he does not do the surgery". He does not yet recognise the problem or the consequences of leaving it untreated, so he has no intention to act: this is Pre-contemplation. Fear alone does not move him forward; awareness of the risk is the missing step, so the doctor's task is education about consequences.
why_wrong_block:
A. Contemplation needs awareness of the problem and its risks with ambivalence about acting. Right if he understood the risks of no surgery but was still weighing his fear against them.
B. Preparation means he intends to proceed soon and is making arrangements (e.g. booking the operation). He is not.
C. Action means the change has been made, i.e. he has undergone or is undergoing the surgery. Not the case here.

Stages of change (Prochaska): match the stage to intention and behaviour, not to how motivated the patient sounds.

  • Preparation: intends to act within the next month and has made a plan or small steps
  • Action: has actually changed the behaviour within the last 6 months
  • Maintenance: change sustained beyond 6 months

exam_pearl: Unaware of the problem or its consequences = Precontemplation; aware but ambivalent = Contemplation.

stem: A 45-year-old smoker came to the clinic for his diabetes follow-up. During discussion, he acknowledged that smoking is not good for his health. He plans to quit this year. According to the Stages of Change Model, at what stage of change is this patient?

stem: A 9-week primigravida vegetarian since 4 years presented to the clinic with concerns about her fetus. Which vitamin is most important to assess?
why_right: Vitamin B12 is found almost only in animal foods (meat, fish, eggs, dairy), so a woman who has been "vegetarian since 4 years" has had time to deplete her stores. In a 9-week pregnancy B12 matters for DNA synthesis, red cell production and fetal neural development; deficiency causes maternal megaloblastic anemia and is linked to neural tube defects and infant developmental delay. So B12 is the vitamin to check.
why_wrong_block:
B. Vitamin K deficiency is rare in adults and pregnancy, and plant foods (leafy greens) supply it well. Its clinical relevance is the newborn (hemorrhagic disease), hence the vitamin K injection at birth.
C. Vitamin C comes from fruit and vegetables, so vegetarians usually have adequate intake. Deficiency (scurvy) is linked to very poor diets, not vegetarianism.
D. Vitamin E deficiency is very rare and is mainly seen with fat malabsorption or in premature infants; vegetable oils and nuts supply it.
key_concept:
Vegetarian or vegan diet = think B12 deficiency (stores last years, so long-standing diets are the risk).
  • B12 sources: meat, fish, eggs, dairy
  • Absorption: terminal ileum, needs intrinsic factor
  • Other B12 risks: gastrectomy, terminal ileum resection or Crohn's, pernicious anemia, metformin
  • Deficiency: megaloblastic anemia, neuropathy; in pregnancy linked to NTDs and infant developmental delay
  • Folate is the other key NTD vitamin, supplemented routinely before and in early pregnancy
exam_pearl: Diet clue "vegetarian/vegan for years" points to B12, not folate (folate is plentiful in leafy plant foods).
compiler_note: Compiler note: AboSarah (UpToDate and ACOG): A pregnant woman vegetarian for several years is at risk of B12 deficiency, especially strict vegetarian/vegan. B12 is essential for DNA synthesis, RBC formation and fetal neural development; deficiency can cause maternal megaloblastic anemia, NTDs or developmental delay in the infant. B12 is found mainly in meat, fish, eggs, dairy. Vit K deficiency rare in pregnancy (newborn hemorrhagic disease). Vit C adequate in vegetarians. Vit E deficiency very rare. In pregnant vegetarians or vegans, always think of B12 deficiency.

stem: A 41 year old woman presents to the clinic requests contraception with no complaints. What is the most appropriate investigation to perform before prescribing contraception? (The Case Didn't Mention Any AUB Or Any Menstrual Irregularities)
key_concept:
Contraception in a healthy woman needs no routine lab or imaging test; investigations are driven by symptoms.
  • No AUB, no complaints: history, exam, BP, then prescribe
  • AUB under 45, no risk factors: TVUS for structural cause
  • AUB at 45 or older: endometrial biopsy
  • AUB under 45 with obesity/PCOS or failed medical therapy: endometrial biopsy
  • Amenorrhea in her 40s: FSH/LH (and TSH, prolactin, pregnancy test)
exam_pearl: Remove the AUB from the stem and every "investigation before contraception" option loses its indication; see the AUB variant (10B).
compiler_note:
Compiler note: No answer marked; compiler wrote '??????'. See 10b for the AUB variant.
⚠ The source marked no answer for this recall (page and next page checked).

stem: A 41 year old woman presents with abnormal uterine bleeding (AUB) For SIX MONTHS and requests contraception. What is the most Important investigation to perform before prescribing contraception?
highlight_terms_source: abnormal uterine bleeding (AUB) For SIX MONTHS
why_right: This recall's key is endometrial biopsy because the woman has "AUB for six months" and is about to start hormonal contraception, which may mask or treat the bleeding. The source reasons that persistent AUB in a woman in her 40s must have endometrial hyperplasia or cancer excluded by tissue before hormones are started, and the lead-in asks for the "most important" test, i.e. the one that rules out malignancy. Persistent AUB is one of the accepted indications for sampling under 45.
why_wrong_block:
A. FSH assesses ovarian reserve or menopausal status (amenorrhea in her 40s). It does not explain or exclude a cause of abnormal bleeding.
B. TSH is part of the general AUB blood work-up for ovulatory dysfunction, but it does not exclude endometrial pathology, which is the key safety question.
C. Ultrasound identifies structural causes (polyps, fibroids) and is the usual first imaging in AUB under 45 without risk factors; it cannot give a tissue diagnosis. The source's alternative answer is ultrasound (see concern).
key_concept:
Endometrial sampling in AUB depends on age and risk.
  • AUB at 45 or older: endometrial biopsy
  • AUB under 45 with unopposed estrogen (obesity, PCOS, poorly controlled diabetes): biopsy
  • AUB under 45 persisting despite medical management: biopsy
  • AUB under 45 without these: TVUS first for structural cause
  • Postmenopausal bleeding: biopsy if endometrial thickness above 5 mm
exam_pearl: Age 41 with no risk factor and no failed treatment is the grey zone: one version of this recall keys TVUS, the other biopsy.
compiler_note:
Compiler note: Compiler's typed version highlights D. Embedded screenshot of the same case (41 year old woman With AUB) gives C. Transvaginal Ultrasound: 'No Indication For Sampling, If She Was 45, Then I Would Choose Sampling'.
Other marked answers: Screenshot (41 y with AUB version): C. Transvaginal Ultrasound

stem: 28 Pregnant in 18 week She came for anomaly scan as routine and they found single umbilical artery" with no congenital anomaly " what to do?
why_right: A single umbilical artery found at the 18-week anomaly scan with "no congenital anomaly" is an isolated finding. Isolated single umbilical artery usually has a normal outcome, because the risk comes from associated anomalies (renal, cardiac, aneuploidy), and the detailed scan has already looked for them. The patient is reassured and continues routine antenatal care; some protocols add a later growth scan because of a small association with growth restriction.
why_wrong_block:
A. Genetic counselling or karyotyping is offered when single umbilical artery comes with other structural anomalies or soft markers suggesting aneuploidy. Isolated, it does not justify invasive testing.
B. Fetal echocardiography is indicated when the anomaly scan cannot show normal cardiac views or other anomalies are present. Here the detailed scan found no anomaly.
D. Termination has no place for an isolated finding with a usually normal prognosis; it would be considered only for severe, lethal anomalies.
key_concept:
Normal cord = 2 arteries + 1 vein; single umbilical artery management depends on whether it is isolated.
  • Isolated (normal anomaly scan): reassure, routine ANC
  • With other anomalies: detailed evaluation, fetal echo, offer karyotype
  • Associations: renal and cardiac anomalies, aneuploidy, growth restriction
  • Maternal association: pregestational diabetes
  • Anomaly scan timing: 18 to 22 weeks
exam_pearl: The phrase "with no congenital anomaly" makes it isolated; add any other anomaly and the answer shifts to further testing.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Other version: A 18 weeks gestation US shows single umbilical artery. A- Reassuring, and continue routine ANC (highlighted) / B- Genetic Test / C- Fetal Echocardiography / D- Close monitoring during pregnancy.

stem: Women with epilepsy is taking lamotrigine. She didn't have seizure attacks since 6 months. She has no personal history of a baby with NTD (neural tubal defect), but her cousin had a baby with spina bifida. What is the recommended folic acid supplementation?
OptB: 5 mg folic acid 3-6 months before pregnancy
highlight_terms_source: no personal history of a baby with NTD
why_right: This recall's key is the standard (average-risk) dose: folic acid 400 micrograms (0.4 mg; the "400 mg" is a unit typo) with multivitamins. The source treats her as average risk because she has no personal history of an NTD-affected baby, a cousin is not a first-degree relative, and she is on lamotrigine, one of the safest antiepileptic drugs in pregnancy and not valproate or carbamazepine. Well-controlled epilepsy (no seizures for 6 months) also means no drug change is needed.
why_wrong_block:
A. High-dose 5 mg is for high NTD risk (previous NTD pregnancy, NTD in her or her partner, first-degree family history, diabetes, hemolytic anemia, some antiepileptics); starting only "during pregnancy" is also too late, as the neural tube closes in the first weeks.
B. Correct timing and dose for a high-risk woman, and many guidelines apply it to all women on antiepileptic drugs (see concern), but the source does not classify a cousin's history plus lamotrigine as high risk.
C. Aspirin is for preeclampsia prophylaxis in high-risk women, not NTD prevention.
key_concept:
Folic acid dose follows NTD risk, started before conception and continued through the first trimester.
  • Average risk: 0.4 mg (400 micrograms) daily
  • High risk (previous NTD, personal/partner NTD, first-degree relative, diabetes, obesity, hemolytic anemia): high dose 4 to 5 mg
  • Valproate and carbamazepine carry the greatest NTD risk
  • Lamotrigine and levetiracetam: safest antiepileptics in pregnancy
  • Sickle cell or thalassemia: high dose throughout pregnancy
exam_pearl: Watch the relative: cousin (second/third degree) is not high risk; mother, sister or a previous child with NTD is.

stem: 31-year-old diabetic woman in active labor. Cardiotocography shows abnormal fetal heart tracing. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
why_right: An "abnormal fetal heart tracing" without features of a terminal tracing is treated as Category 2 (non-reassuring), managed by stepwise intrauterine resuscitation. The lead-in asks for the "next step", and the first step is lateral repositioning of the mother, which relieves aortocaval compression and improves uteroplacental blood flow. All the other options are valid later steps.
why_wrong_block:
A. Stopping oxytocin is step 3, after repositioning and oxygen/fluids; it is first priority only when uterine hyperstimulation is the clear cause. The stem does not mention oxytocin.
B. Oxygen with IV fluids is step 2, used after the mother has been repositioned.
C. A tocolytic is the last step, for persistent tachysystole or a tracing that fails to improve with the earlier measures.
key_concept:
Category 2 CTG: intrauterine resuscitation in a fixed order.
  • Step 1: lateral repositioning of the mother
  • Step 2: oxygen and IV fluids
  • Step 3: stop oxytocin
  • Step 4: tocolytic
  • Category 3 or no improvement: expedite delivery
exam_pearl: When every option is a correct action, pick the earliest in the sequence: reposition first.

stem: Women underwent pelvic smear, it showed Atypical Glandular Cells (AGC). What is the most appropriate management?
why_right: Atypical glandular cells (AGC) carry a substantial risk of significant pathology (high-grade cervical lesions, adenocarcinoma of the cervix or endometrium), regardless of HPV status. All AGC results therefore go straight to colposcopy with endocervical sampling, plus endometrial sampling in older women or those with risk factors. HPV triage is not used for AGC.
why_wrong_block: A. Reflex HPV testing triages ASC-US in women 25 or older; a negative HPV result does not exclude glandular or endometrial disease, so it cannot replace colposcopy for AGC.
key_concept:
Pap result decides the next step.
  • Unsatisfactory: repeat Pap in 2 to 4 months
  • ASC-US 25 or older: HPV test; positive then colposcopy
  • ASC-US or LSIL 21 to 24: repeat Pap in 1 year
  • LSIL 25 or older, ASC-H, HSIL: colposcopy
  • AGC: colposcopy with endocervical sampling, plus endometrial sampling if older or at risk
exam_pearl: Only ASC-US is triaged by HPV; glandular atypia always goes to colposcopy.

stem: Primigravida in labor was given oxytocin then ctg showed recurrent late deceleration and reduced variability. Which of the following is the management
highlight_terms_source: recurrent late deceleration and reduced variability
why_right: Recurrent late decelerations with reduced (not absent) variability is a Category 2 (non-reassuring) tracing, and the clue is that it appeared after oxytocin was given. Oxytocin drives strong, frequent contractions that cut uteroplacental flow, so the cause-directed fix is to stop the oxytocin; this is the step of intrauterine resuscitation that removes the trigger.
why_wrong_block:
A. CS: a Category 2 trace is first treated with intrauterine resuscitation; caesarean is for Category 3 (absent variability with recurrent decelerations, bradycardia) or a trace that fails to recover.
B. Change maternal position: the first generic step for a Category 2 trace with no obvious cause; here the stem points to oxytocin as the cause, so stopping it is the key management.
C. Oxygenation: oxygen and IV fluids are a supportive step, but they do not remove the oxytocin-induced hyperstimulation that is causing the late decelerations.
key_concept:
Category 2 CTG: intrauterine resuscitation before delivery.
  • Step 1: lateral repositioning
  • Step 2: oxygen and IV fluids
  • Step 3: stop oxytocin
  • Step 4: tocolytic
  • Late decels = uteroplacental insufficiency (oxytocin, epidural hypotension)
  • Category 3 or failed resuscitation: expedite delivery
exam_pearl: If the stem names oxytocin as the trigger, stop it; if no cause is given and the lead-in is 'first step', reposition the mother.

stem: A 32 years old G3 presented with PROM At 33 for 4 hours , no uterine contraction , vitally stable. She was given IV antibiotics and admitted under observation. There Was No Abdominal Pain Or Fever (Written In The Question Like This) Which of the following neonatal complication will be reduced after IV antibiotic?
why_right: In PPROM at 33 weeks, IV latency antibiotics are given to prevent ascending infection (chorioamnionitis) and to prolong the time to delivery. Their direct neonatal benefit is a reduction in neonatal infection/sepsis, which is what the lead-in 'reduced after IV antibiotic' targets.
why_wrong_block:
B. Retinopathy: retinopathy of prematurity relates to extreme prematurity and oxygen exposure; antibiotics have no specific effect on it.
C. Intracranial hemorrhage: intraventricular hemorrhage is reduced by antenatal corticosteroids, not by antibiotics; MgSO4 below 32 weeks targets cerebral palsy (neuroprotection), not IVH.
D. Respiratory distress syndrome: RDS is the outcome prevented by antenatal corticosteroids; antibiotics may help only indirectly by prolonging latency, which is why some recalls key RDS, but infection is the direct target.
key_concept:
PPROM: match each drug to the neonatal outcome it reduces.
  • Antibiotics (ampicillin plus erythromycin): infection/sepsis, chorioamnionitis, longer latency
  • Corticosteroids (<34 weeks): RDS, IVH, NEC
  • MgSO4 (<32 weeks): cerebral palsy (neuroprotection)
exam_pearl: 'Antibiotic reduces' = infection; 'steroid reduces' = RDS. The drug in the lead-in decides the answer.
compiler_note:
Compiler note: Compiler highlights A. Embedded screenshot of the same question gives D. Respiratory distress syndrome.
Other marked answers: Screenshot: D. Respiratory distress syndrome

stem: pregnant at 1st visit, height and weight was provided. And Said "She Has Positive Family History For Type 2 Diabetes" and ask at what bmi you Would do screening for diabetes mellitus?
highlight_terms_source: Positive Family History For Type 2 Diabetes
why_right: At the first antenatal visit, women with risk factors are screened early for pre-existing (undiagnosed) diabetes. The guideline trigger is being overweight, BMI ≥25, plus at least one additional risk factor, and a first-degree family history of type 2 diabetes is exactly that additional factor here, so a BMI of 25 is enough to screen.
why_wrong_block:
B. 30: obesity is the threshold used when no other risk factor is present; with a positive family history the bar drops to 25.
C. 35: this is a bariatric surgery threshold (with comorbidities), not a diabetes screening cut-off.
D. 40: a bariatric surgery threshold (severe obesity); waiting for this BMI would miss most women who need screening.
key_concept:
Early diabetes screening at booking depends on BMI plus risk factors.
  • BMI ≥25 + one risk factor (first-degree relative with diabetes, previous GDM, PCOS, hypertension, previous macrosomia): screen
  • No other risk factor: obesity (BMI ≥30) is the trigger
  • Previous GDM: screen early regardless of BMI
  • Everyone else: routine screening at 24 to 28 weeks
exam_pearl: Family history present = 25; 'no risk factors' stated = 30.

stem: pregnant at 1st visit, height and weight was provided. Then Said "She Has No Risk Factors" (Literally Stated In The Stem) and ask at what bmi you Would do screening for diabetes mellitus?
why_right: The stem stresses 'she has no risk factors'. The BMI ≥25 threshold only applies when an additional risk factor exists, so without one, obesity (BMI ≥30) is itself the risk factor that justifies screening for diabetes in pregnancy.
why_wrong_block:
A. 25: overweight alone is not enough; 25 is the cut-off only when combined with another risk factor such as a first-degree relative with diabetes.
C. 35: a bariatric surgery threshold (with comorbidities), not a screening cut-off; obesity starts at 30.
D. 40: severe obesity and a bariatric surgery threshold; far too high for diabetes screening.
key_concept:
Which BMI triggers diabetes screening in pregnancy?
  • Risk factor present (family history, previous GDM, PCOS): BMI ≥25
  • No other risk factor: BMI ≥30 (obesity)
  • 35 and 40 belong to bariatric surgery criteria
  • Previous GDM: screen early whatever the BMI
exam_pearl: The words 'no risk factors' move the answer from 25 to 30.

stem: pregnant at 1st vist, hieght and weight was provided and ask at what bmi you Would do screening for diabetes mellietus? (General Question , Didn't Mention "Family History" And Didn't Mention "No Risk Factors")
why_right: This recall's key is 25 because the BMI cut-off quoted in diabetes screening guidance is overweight, BMI ≥25, at which a woman with any additional risk factor is screened at booking. With the stem silent on risk factors, the recall takes the guideline number itself as the answer.
why_wrong_block:
B. 30: obesity is the trigger when the stem explicitly says there are no other risk factors (as in the paired recall); the general guideline figure is 25.
C. 35: a bariatric surgery threshold (with comorbidities), not a diabetes screening cut-off.
D. 40: a bariatric surgery threshold for severe obesity; not used for diabetes screening.
key_concept:
Three versions of the same recall, three triggers.
  • Family history stated: 25
  • 'No risk factors' stated: 30
  • General question, nothing stated: 25 (guideline overweight cut-off)
  • 35 and 40 are bariatric numbers, never the answer here
exam_pearl: Read the stem for the risk-factor phrase: present or silent = 25, explicitly absent = 30.

stem: 36-week pregnant woman, G4P3, presents with a fetus in breech presentation. What is the best time to perform an external cephalic version (ECV)?
why_right: ECV is offered once the pregnancy is term (from 37 weeks): by then spontaneous version is less likely, and if a complication forces delivery the baby is mature. This woman is G4P3 (multiparous), and multiparas are commonly offered ECV from 37 weeks, so at 36 weeks the best plan is to wait until 37 weeks.
why_wrong_block:
A. 36 weeks: the time to offer ECV to a nulliparous woman; in a multipara the breech may still turn spontaneously, so wait until 37 weeks.
C. 38 weeks: ECV can still be attempted later, but success falls as liquor reduces and the breech engages, and labour may begin first; 37 weeks is the planned time.
D. At time of delivery: ECV is contraindicated once labour is established with ruptured membranes or a need for urgent delivery; it is a planned antenatal procedure.
key_concept:
ECV timing and exclusions.
  • Nulliparous: from 36 weeks; multiparous: from 37 weeks
  • Done near theatre with CTG before and after
  • Exclusions: significant third-trimester bleeding, placenta praevia, multiple pregnancy, non-reassuring CTG, uterine malformation, ruptured membranes
exam_pearl: If the alternate stem adds vaginal bleeding that will not stop, ECV is contraindicated and the question becomes delivery, not timing.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Alternate recall (Q:): gravida 36 weeks came with vaginal bleeding, retained and treatment given but bleeding didn't stop, baby breech; at what time you will perform ECV? Vitals and labs not given. Options: A now, B 37 weeks (highlighted), C 39 weeks, D 40 weeks.

stem: 21-year-old primigravida is currently at 20 weeks gestation. Her past medical history is significant for mitral stenosis secondary to rheumatic heart disease as a child. What physiologic change places her at risk for the development of heart failure during pregnancy?
why_right: With a fixed, narrow mitral valve, pregnancy's rise in blood volume and stroke volume (cardiac output) must all cross the stenotic valve. Left atrial pressure rises, causing pulmonary congestion and heart failure; the risk peaks when cardiac output peaks (late second and third trimester, labour, immediately postpartum).
why_wrong_block:
A. Increase in red cell mass: red cells rise less than plasma (dilutional anaemia); it is the total volume and output load, not red cell mass, that decompensates a stenotic valve.
C. Increase in minute ventilation: progesterone-driven hyperventilation causes mild respiratory alkalosis and physiological breathlessness, not cardiac volume overload.
D. Increase in renal plasma flow: it raises GFR and lowers creatinine and urea; it does not load the left atrium.
key_concept:
Mitral stenosis is the valve lesion with the worst prognosis in pregnancy.
  • Rising blood volume and stroke volume raise left atrial pressure
  • Tachycardia shortens diastolic filling, worsening the gradient
  • Danger points: third trimester, labour, immediately postpartum
  • Regurgitant lesions tolerate pregnancy better (lower SVR)
exam_pearl: Stenosis = fixed outflow that cannot handle more volume; regurgitation improves with falling SVR.

stem: Old female presented with ascites, and pleural effusion. On US, there is adnexal mass. What is the diagnosis?
why_right: An older woman with an adnexal mass plus ascites and pleural effusion has the advanced picture of ovarian cancer: peritoneal spread produces ascites and transdiaphragmatic spread produces a (usually right-sided) pleural effusion. Age and ascites both favour a malignant adnexal mass.
why_wrong_block:
B. Cervical cancer: presents with postcoital or irregular bleeding and a cervical lesion; it spreads locally to the parametrium (hydronephrosis), not as an adnexal mass with ascites.
C. Endometrial cancer: presents early with postmenopausal bleeding and a bulky uterus, not with an adnexal mass and ascites.
D. Uterine cancer: arises in the uterus itself (endometrium or sarcoma) and gives bleeding or an enlarging uterus, not an adnexal mass.
key_concept:
Ovarian cancer: silent until advanced.
  • Early: bloating, early satiety, pain, weight loss
  • Advanced: ascites, pleural effusion, adnexal (often bilateral) masses, raised CA-125
  • First test TVUS, then CA-125; CT for staging
  • Definitive diagnosis: histopathology at surgical staging
exam_pearl: Ascites plus pleural effusion with a benign solid ovarian fibroma is Meigs syndrome; in an older woman assume malignancy until proven otherwise.

stem: A 20-year-old woman at 6 weeks gestation is receiving methotrexate treatment for an ectopic pregnancy. The first dose of methotrexate 50 mg/m² IM was administered one week ago. The human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG) levels on days 1, 4, and 7 were as follows: Day 1: 1000 mIU/mL Day 4: 1200 mIU/mL Day 7: 1100 mIU/mL Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
OptD: Administer a second dose of methotrexate
why_right: After single-dose methotrexate the response is judged from day 4 to day 7: here hCG goes from 1200 to 1100, a fall of under 10%, i.e. a plateau or decrease <15%. That is an inadequate response, and the protocol is to give a second dose of methotrexate in a stable patient. The day 1 to day 4 rise (1000 to 1200) is expected and should be ignored.
why_wrong_block:
A. Weekly hCG follow-up is only for an adequate response, a fall of more than 15% between day 4 and day 7 (as in 1200 to 800).
B. Immediate surgery is for a rising hCG after methotrexate or haemodynamic instability or rupture; here hCG fell slightly and she is stable.
C. After a suboptimal single-dose response the next step is a second single dose, not switching to an inpatient multiple-dose regimen.
key_concept:
After single-dose methotrexate, judge the response on the day 4 vs day 7 hCG, never day 1 vs day 7.
  • Day 1 to day 4 rise: expected, ignore
  • Fall >15% (day 4 to 7): weekly hCG until undetectable
  • Plateau or fall <15%: second methotrexate dose
  • Rising hCG: treatment failure, surgery (laparoscopic salpingectomy or salpingostomy)
  • Unstable or signs of rupture at any point: immediate surgery
exam_pearl: Comparing day 1 with day 7 (1000 vs 1100) looks like a rise and tempts surgery; the rule uses day 4 vs day 7.

stem: A Woman Presents With A Complaint Of Decreased Fetal Movement At 24 weeks of gestation. Ultrasound: Fetal Demise. How would you manage?
why_right: Fetal death at 24 weeks is an IUFD (≥20 weeks), and the uterus must be evacuated by induction. Below 28 weeks misoprostol is the most effective single agent for this, because the uterus is relatively insensitive to oxytocin in the second trimester and misoprostol both ripens the cervix and causes contractions.
why_wrong_block:
A. Oxytocin: few oxytocin receptors in the mid-trimester uterus make it ineffective alone; it is used for IUFD later in pregnancy (third trimester) or after a favourable cervix.
C. Mifepristone: an antiprogestogen used as priming 24 to 48 hours before misoprostol to shorten induction; it does not complete the evacuation on its own.
D. Dinoprostone: a PGE2 used mainly for cervical ripening at term; for second-trimester demise misoprostol is more effective, cheaper and stable.
key_concept:
Pregnancy loss: gestation decides the method.
  • <20 weeks = abortion; ≥20 weeks = IUFD
  • Missed abortion <13 weeks: expectant, misoprostol, or surgical evacuation
  • IUFD <28 weeks: misoprostol (mifepristone priming optional)
  • IUFD in third trimester: standard induction (prostaglandin, oxytocin)
exam_pearl: Mifepristone primes, misoprostol delivers; pick misoprostol when only one drug can be chosen.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Alternate recall (Q:): same, ultrasound shows No Fetal Heart Beat; B Misoprostol highlighted.

stem: A Female (33–35 Weeks Gestation) Presented With Rupture Of Membranes (ROM) for more than 24 hours. She Was Asked About Which Antibiotics Should Be Used To Prevent Post- Delivery Pelvic Infections.
highlight_terms_source: Rupture Of Membranes (ROM) for more than 24 hours
why_right: This recall's key is vancomycin, likely reasoning that prolonged rupture of membranes (>24 hours) raises the risk of ascending infection, including Group B streptococcus, and that vancomycin is the reserve GBS agent. That reasoning is weak: vancomycin is used for GBS prophylaxis only in severe penicillin allergy with a clindamycin-resistant isolate, and it is not a standard regimen for preventing postpartum pelvic infection.
why_wrong_block:
B. Ceftriaxone: not a recommended prophylactic agent here; the cephalosporin used for surgical prophylaxis at caesarean is cefazolin.
C. Clindamycin and gentamicin: the classic regimen to treat established postpartum endometritis, not to prevent it.
D. Azithromycin and metronidazole: azithromycin is a recognised adjunct (with cefazolin) at caesarean after labour or ruptured membranes and an alternative to erythromycin in PPROM, but this pairing is not a standard regimen.
key_concept:
Antibiotics around ruptured membranes.
  • PPROM latency: ampicillin plus erythromycin (azithromycin alternative)
  • GBS positive or unknown with risk factors: intrapartum IV penicillin or ampicillin
  • Severe penicillin allergy: clindamycin if sensitive, otherwise vancomycin
  • Caesarean after labour/ROM: cefazolin plus adjunctive azithromycin
  • Chorioamnionitis: ampicillin plus gentamicin and delivery
  • Postpartum endometritis treatment: clindamycin plus gentamicin
exam_pearl: Treat endometritis = clindamycin plus gentamicin; prevent it = prophylaxis (cefazolin, plus azithromycin if in labour or after ROM).
compiler_note: Compiler note: Alternate recall (Q:): 37-weeks patient to labor room with PROM for 24 hours, how to prevent postpartum pelvic infection? (C-section not mentioned): A Vancomycin (highlighted), B Clindamycin, C Clindamycin Plus Gentamicin, D Amoxicillin Plus Metronidazole.

stem: A Female (33–35 Weeks Gestation) Presented With Rupture Of Membranes (ROM) for more than 24 hours. She Was Asked About Which Antibiotics Should Be Used To TREAT Post- Delivery Pelvic Infections. (C-Section Not Mentioned)
why_right: The lead-in asks how to TREAT a post-delivery pelvic infection after ROM for more than 24 hours, which is the classic setup for postpartum endometritis (prolonged ROM is a major risk factor for intra-amniotic and uterine infection). Postpartum endometritis is polymicrobial (anaerobes plus Gram-negative and Gram-positive aerobes), so treatment needs broad IV cover: clindamycin plus gentamicin is the standard regimen. Antibiotics are continued until the patient is afebrile and clinically improved.
why_wrong_block:
A. Vancomycin covers only Gram-positive organisms (including MRSA); it misses the anaerobes and Gram-negative rods that drive endometritis. It is added only for specific situations such as known MRSA.
B. Ceftriaxone alone gives poor anaerobic cover, so it is inadequate for polymicrobial pelvic infection. It is the drug for gonorrhea, not for postpartum endometritis.
D. Azithromycin plus metronidazole is not a recognized treatment regimen for endometritis and leaves Gram-negative aerobes poorly covered. Azithromycin is used as an adjunct to cesarean prophylaxis or for chlamydia; metronidazole for BV or trichomonas.
key_concept:
Postpartum endometritis = polymicrobial: treat with IV clindamycin + gentamicin.
  • Risk factors: prolonged ROM, prolonged labor, cesarean delivery, repeated vaginal exams, chorioamnionitis
  • Picture: fever, uterine tenderness, foul lochia after delivery
  • Intrapartum chorioamnionitis: ampicillin + gentamicin AND deliver
  • Post-delivery endometritis: clindamycin + gentamicin until afebrile
  • Prophylaxis (prevent) is a different question from treatment
exam_pearl: Lead-in verb decides it: TREAT a postpartum pelvic infection = clindamycin + gentamicin; intrapartum chorioamnionitis = ampicillin + gentamicin plus delivery.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Q: recall inside the 70 block asking about TREATMENT (vs prevention in 70).

stem: A Female (33–35 Weeks Gestation) Presented With Rupture Of Membranes (ROM) for more than 6 hours. She Is Planned For C-Section. She Was Asked About Which Antibiotics Should Be Used To Prevent Post- Delivery Pelvic Infections.
why_right: This recall's key is clindamycin plus gentamicin: the woman has ROM for more than 6 hours and is going for C-section, so she carries a high risk of post-delivery endometritis and wound infection, and the source chose the broad combination that covers the polymicrobial pelvic flora (anaerobes plus Gram-negatives). Among the listed options it is the only combination that gives that breadth of cover.
why_wrong_block:
A. Vancomycin is Gram-positive only and is not used as routine cesarean prophylaxis; it is added only for known MRSA colonization.
B. Clindamycin alone misses Gram-negative aerobes; in beta-lactam allergy it must be paired with an aminoglycoside (gentamicin), which is exactly option C.
D. Azithromycin plus metronidazole is not a standard prophylactic regimen. Azithromycin is used only as an ADD-ON to a cephalosporin in labor or after ROM, and metronidazole is for BV or trichomonas.
key_concept:
Cesarean prophylaxis: give before skin incision; broaden when in labor or membranes ruptured.
  • Standard: single-dose IV cefazolin before incision
  • In labor / ROM: add adjunctive azithromycin to cefazolin
  • Beta-lactam allergy: clindamycin + gentamicin
  • Treatment of endometritis: clindamycin + gentamicin
  • Prolonged ROM raises the risk of chorioamnionitis and endometritis
exam_pearl: If cefazolin appears among the options, it is the routine cesarean prophylaxis; clindamycin + gentamicin is the allergy alternative and the treatment regimen.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Alternate recall (Q:): woman had vaginal delivery at term with prolonged rupture of membranes (24 hours); question asked about prevention; options included A Vancomycin, B Clindamycin + gentamicin (highlighted).

stem: 59-year-old postmenopausal woman with a history of breast cancer on tamoxifen Presents with 2 months of abnormal vaginal bleeding. An endometrial biopsy was attempted but inadequate. What is the most appropriate in management?
highlight_terms_source: endometrial biopsy was attempted but inadequate
why_right: A postmenopausal woman on tamoxifen with 2 months of bleeding must have endometrial cancer excluded, because tamoxifen acts as an estrogen agonist on the endometrium and raises the risk of hyperplasia, polyps and carcinoma. The office biopsy was inadequate, so the next step is hysteroscopy with directed biopsy, which views the cavity and samples focal lesions (such as polyps) that a blind biopsy can miss.
why_wrong_block:
A. Stopping tamoxifen does not diagnose the cause of the bleeding and would interrupt her breast cancer therapy; that decision comes after tissue diagnosis with the oncologist.
C. Hysterectomy without a tissue diagnosis is premature; it would be right once atypical hyperplasia or carcinoma is confirmed.
D. TVUS is the usual first test in postmenopausal bleeding, but on tamoxifen the endometrial thickness is unreliable (subendometrial cystic change), and a scan cannot give the tissue diagnosis that the inadequate biopsy failed to provide; a reassuring scan would not end the work-up.
key_concept:
Postmenopausal bleeding: tissue diagnosis is mandatory; if office biopsy fails or is inadequate, go to hysteroscopy + directed biopsy.
  • Postmenopausal bleeding + endometrium >5 mm on TVUS: biopsy
  • Tamoxifen: endometrial agonist, so higher risk of polyps, hyperplasia, cancer
  • Tamoxifen distorts TVUS thickness, so bleeding needs histology
  • Blind biopsy can miss focal lesions; hysteroscopy sees and samples them
  • Hysterectomy only after histology confirms atypia or cancer
exam_pearl: Inadequate or negative biopsy with persistent postmenopausal bleeding is never the end point: proceed to hysteroscopy.

stem: Pregnant came with BP 150/90, lower limb edema. Asking about next step in management?
OptA: Reassurance as edema normal in pregnancy
OptB: Admit for further evaluation and rule out preeclampsia
why_right: BP 150/90 in pregnancy is hypertensive (140/90 or more), and with lower limb edema preeclampsia must be excluded rather than dismissed. The next step is further evaluation: confirm the BP, check urine for proteinuria and send labs for end-organ dysfunction (platelets, liver enzymes, creatinine). Edema itself is common in pregnancy, but the raised BP is what makes reassurance unsafe.
why_wrong_block: A. Edema alone can be physiological in pregnancy, but here it comes with a BP of 150/90, so reassurance would miss possible preeclampsia. Reassurance fits only isolated edema with normal BP and no proteinuria.
key_concept:
Hypertension in pregnancy: confirm and classify before treating.
  • Chronic HTN: before 20 weeks or pre-pregnancy
  • Gestational HTN: new after 20 weeks, no proteinuria or end-organ damage
  • Preeclampsia: new after 20 weeks + proteinuria or end-organ dysfunction
  • Severe range: 160/110 or higher, treat urgently
  • Edema is NOT a diagnostic criterion for preeclampsia
exam_pearl: High BP + edema = work-up for preeclampsia (proteinuria, labs); never reassure just because edema is common in pregnancy.

stem: A 30 years old women diabetic for 15 years presented in antenatal clinic for preconception. Her HbA1c is 8.2. What to do?
OptA: Low dose aspirin for pregnancy complications prevention
why_right: She is preconception with long-standing diabetes and an HbA1c of 8.2. Poor periconceptional glycemic control is the main modifiable driver of congenital anomalies and miscarriage in pregestational diabetes, so the priority is to optimize control to the target HbA1c below 6.5% before she conceives, using effective contraception until the target is reached.
why_wrong_block:
A. Low-dose aspirin is for preeclampsia prevention and is started during pregnancy from about 12 weeks, not preconception; it does nothing for her uncontrolled glucose.
B. Folic acid is also given before conception (high-dose in diabetes), but it does not address the main risk shown by the stem, an HbA1c of 8.2; it is an add-on, not the key step.
key_concept:
Pregestational diabetes preconception care: control glucose first, then conceive.
  • Target HbA1c below 6.5% before and during pregnancy
  • Contraception until the target is reached
  • Folic acid preconception (higher dose advised in diabetes)
  • Aspirin from about 12 weeks to reduce preeclampsia risk
  • Screen for retinopathy and nephropathy; review teratogenic drugs
exam_pearl: Raised HbA1c in a woman planning pregnancy: the answer is glycemic control before conception, not supplements.

stem: A pregnant woman with diabetes mellitus and obesity is being evaluated for obstetric risk Which of the following is the most appropriate maneuver to help prevent shoulder dystocia during delivery?
why_right: Diabetes and obesity raise the risk of fetal macrosomia and therefore shoulder dystocia. No manoeuvre truly prevents dystocia; the lead-in really asks which manoeuvre you use first to relieve the impacted shoulder at delivery. Of the listed options, suprapubic pressure (together with McRoberts) is the first-line, simplest and safest step: pressure just above the pubic bone pushes the anterior shoulder down and inward so it slips under the symphysis. The other options are second-line or last-resort manoeuvres.
why_wrong_block:
A. Rubin manoeuvre is an internal rotational manoeuvre (pressure on the posterior aspect of the anterior shoulder); it is second-line, used when McRoberts and suprapubic pressure fail.
C. Gaskin (all-fours) manoeuvre is an alternative used when first-line manoeuvres fail, especially in mobile women without an epidural; it is not the initial step.
D. Zavanelli manoeuvre (pushing the head back for cesarean) is the last resort after all other manoeuvres fail, with high maternal and fetal morbidity.
key_concept:
Shoulder dystocia ladder: call for help, then external manoeuvres, then internal, then last resort.
  • First line: McRoberts (hyperflex thighs) + suprapubic pressure
  • Second line: internal rotation (Rubin, Woods screw) or deliver posterior arm
  • Alternative: Gaskin all-fours position
  • Last resort: Zavanelli, symphysiotomy, cleidotomy
  • Never apply fundal pressure
  • Risks: macrosomia, diabetes, obesity, prior dystocia
exam_pearl: Suprapubic pressure, NOT fundal pressure: fundal pressure impacts the shoulder further.

stem: Pt female came for birth control she had previous DVT, what contraception u give?
why_right: A previous DVT makes all estrogen-containing methods contraindicated, because estrogen increases the risk of venous thromboembolism. An IUD (copper, or levonorgestrel which is progestin-only) carries no meaningful thrombotic risk and is highly effective, so it is the method of choice.
why_wrong_block:
A. The transdermal patch contains estrogen (and gives a high estrogen exposure), so it carries the same VTE risk as the combined pill and is contraindicated after DVT.
C. The combined OCP contains estrogen and increases DVT and PE risk; it is contraindicated with a history of VTE. A progestin-only pill would be acceptable.
key_concept:
History of VTE: no estrogen.
  • Contraindicated: combined pill, patch, vaginal ring
  • Safe choices: copper IUD, LNG-IUD, implant, progestin-only pill
  • Copper IUD: no hormones at all
  • Main IUD side effect: abnormal uterine bleeding
  • Estrogen also avoided in the first 6 weeks postpartum (VTE risk) and generally in breastfeeding (suppresses milk)
exam_pearl: Patch and ring are estrogen methods too: a DVT history excludes them just like the combined pill.

stem: 24-week pregnant woman presents with exertional dyspnea. She is otherwise healthy, and systemic examination is unremarkable. Ultrasound shows monochorionic twin pregnancy with evidence of twin-to-twin transfusion syndrome (TTTS). What is the most appropriate next step in Management?
OptC: Laser photocoagulation of placental vascular anastomoses
why_right: TTTS in monochorionic twins arises from unbalanced vascular anastomoses on the shared placenta; untreated progressive disease carries very high perinatal mortality. At 24 weeks (within the roughly 16 to 26 week window) the definitive treatment is fetoscopic laser photocoagulation of the anastomoses, which treats the cause and improves survival and neurological outcome. Her exertional dyspnea fits uterine overdistension from polyhydramnios in the recipient twin.
why_wrong_block:
A. Termination is not the standard answer when an effective fetal therapy exists; it is a counselling option in severe or late-detected disease only.
B. Expectant observation with close ultrasound surveillance is reasonable only for early, stable disease (Quintero stage I); established TTTS needs laser.
D. Cesarean at 24 weeks means extreme prematurity; delivery is considered only at later gestations or when fetal therapy is not possible.
key_concept:
TTTS: monochorionic twins, donor (oligohydramnios, small bladder) vs recipient (polyhydramnios, overload).
  • Stage I, stable: close surveillance
  • Stage II to IV, roughly 16 to 26 weeks: fetoscopic laser ablation
  • Beyond the laser window: amnioreduction, then delivery planning
  • Screen monochorionic twins with ultrasound every 2 weeks from 16 weeks
exam_pearl: Dichorionic twins cannot get TTTS; the key word is "monochorionic".
compiler_note:
Repeats: appears 2× in this file (also AS-0431).
Compiler note: Alternate recall (Q:): same at 22-week; C Laser photocoagulation highlighted.

stem: 12-week pregnant woman presents with exertional dyspnea. She is otherwise healthy, and systemic examination is unremarkable. Ultrasound shows monochorionic twin pregnancy with evidence of twin-to-twin transfusion syndrome (TTTS). What is the most appropriate next step in Management?
OptC: Laser photocoagulation of placental vascular anastomoses
why_right: At only 12 weeks, a monochorionic pregnancy with TTTS features is managed with expectant management and close ultrasound surveillance. Fetoscopic laser ablation is performed in the window of about 16 to 26 weeks, so it is not yet an option, and there is no indication for delivery or termination. The exertional dyspnea with a normal examination is physiological breathlessness of pregnancy, not a maternal complication.
why_wrong_block:
A. Termination is not the default; it may be discussed only for severe, untreatable disease after counselling, not as the next step in an otherwise healthy woman.
C. Laser photocoagulation of the placental anastomoses is the treatment for significant TTTS (stage II or more) between about 16 and 26 weeks; at 12 weeks it is too early.
D. Cesarean section is a delivery method; at 12 weeks the pregnancy is far from viable and there is no indication to deliver.
key_concept:
Monochorionic twins: surveillance from early pregnancy; TTTS treatment depends on gestation and stage.
  • Monochorionic: serial ultrasound every 2 weeks from about 16 weeks
  • TTTS: donor oligohydramnios, recipient polyhydramnios
  • Laser ablation: stage II or higher, about 16 to 26 weeks
  • Amnioreduction: option for later gestations or as a temporary measure
  • Too early for laser: observe and re-scan
exam_pearl: Gestational age decides it: before the laser window, the answer is observation, not intervention.

stem: Fishy Smell Vaginal Discharge With Clue Cells And Positive Whiff Test — Diagnosis?
highlight_terms_source: Clue Cells And Positive Whiff Test
why_right: Fishy smell, clue cells and a positive whiff test (fishy amine odor when KOH is added) are the diagnostic features of bacterial vaginosis, caused by overgrowth of Gardnerella and anaerobes with loss of lactobacilli. The discharge is thin and gray-white with pH above 4.5. Treatment is metronidazole for the patient only.
why_wrong_block:
A. Candida gives a thick, white, curdy, odorless discharge with itching, pseudohyphae on KOH, normal pH and a negative whiff test.
B. Trichomonas can smell foul and be whiff-positive, but it gives a frothy yellow-green discharge, strawberry cervix and motile flagellated protozoa on wet prep, not clue cells.
key_concept:
Vaginitis by microscopy:
  • BV: clue cells, whiff +, pH above 4.5, thin gray fishy discharge; metronidazole, partner not treated
  • Trichomonas: motile flagellates, frothy yellow-green, strawberry cervix; metronidazole + treat partner
  • Candida: pseudohyphae, curdy odorless, pH normal; azoles
  • Amsel criteria for BV: 3 of 4 (discharge, pH, whiff, clue cells)
exam_pearl: Clue cells point to BV; motile flagellates point to trichomonas, even if both smell fishy.

stem: 28-Week Pregnant Woman With Cough And Dyspnea, Bilateral Rhonchi, Allergy History — Most Appropriate Initial Test?
why_right: Cough and dyspnea with bilateral rhonchi in a woman with an allergy history points to asthma. The lead-in asks for the initial test, and spirometry is the diagnostic test of choice: it shows obstructive airflow (reduced FEV1/FVC) with reversibility after a bronchodilator. It is non-invasive and safe at 28 weeks.
why_wrong_block:
B. Chest X-ray does not diagnose asthma; it is used when pneumonia or a complication such as pneumothorax is suspected (fever, focal crackles).
C. ABG assesses severity in a severe or life-threatening exacerbation with respiratory distress; it is not the initial diagnostic test.
D. Hemoglobin estimation looks for anemia, which can cause dyspnea but does not explain rhonchi, cough and atopy.
key_concept:
Suspected asthma: spirometry with bronchodilator reversibility.
  • Obstruction: FEV1/FVC below 0.7
  • Reversibility: FEV1 rise of 12% or more after bronchodilator
  • Normal spirometry but high suspicion: methacholine challenge
  • Spirometry and inhaled therapy are safe in pregnancy
  • CXR only if pneumonia or complications suspected
exam_pearl: Atopy + cough + dyspnea + bilateral rhonchi = asthma: spirometry first, even in pregnancy.

stem: Most common subtype HPV in cervical cancer?
why_right: HPV 16 and 18 are the high-risk oncogenic types and together cause the large majority (about 70%) of cervical cancers worldwide. HPV 16 is the single most common type, mainly in squamous cell carcinoma, while HPV 18 is relatively more frequent in adenocarcinoma. Their E6 and E7 oncoproteins inactivate p53 and Rb, driving dysplasia.
why_wrong_block:
A. The pair given (11/12) is not a cervical cancer pair; HPV 6 and 11 are the low-risk types causing genital warts and recurrent respiratory papillomatosis, and HPV 12 is not a genital type.
C. HPV 31 and 33 are high-risk types that can cause cancer, but they are far less common than 16 and 18; 32 and 36 are not recognised cervical cancer types.
D. HPV 44 is a low-risk type associated with benign genital lesions; it is not a significant cause of cervical cancer.
key_concept:
HPV types: high risk = cancer, low risk = warts.
  • 16: most common overall, squamous cell carcinoma
  • 18: relatively more adenocarcinoma
  • 16 + 18 together: about 70% of cervical cancers
  • 6 and 11: genital warts, laryngeal papillomas (low risk)
  • Other high risk: 31, 33, 45, 52, 58 (covered by the 9-valent vaccine)
  • Oncogenesis: E6 degrades p53, E7 inactivates Rb
exam_pearl: Warts = 6/11; cancer = 16/18. Do not mix the two pairs.
compiler_note: Repeats: appears 2× in this file (also AS-0263).

stem: A 22 years old woman with a history of multiple sexual transmitted diseases presented at the 37th gestational week for her first antenatal visit. The obstetrician is concerned about this maternal infection, which may cause conjunctivitis and blindness in the newborn. Which of the following is the most suitable for health promotion and illness prevention?
highlight_terms_source: conjunctivitis and blindness in the newborn
key_concept:
Maternal STI causing neonatal eye disease: treat the mother before delivery.
  • Chlamydia: most common cause of neonatal conjunctivitis; onset about 5 to 14 days; may also cause pneumonia
  • Gonorrhea: onset 2 to 5 days, purulent, can perforate the cornea and cause blindness
  • Chlamydia in pregnancy: azithromycin (doxycycline avoided)
  • Gonorrhea in pregnancy: ceftriaxone
  • All newborns: ocular prophylaxis at birth
exam_pearl: Health promotion and prevention in the stem usually points to acting on the mother before delivery, not waiting to screen the baby.

stem: A 30-year-old woman with a history of infertility for 6 years complains of severe dysmenorrhea unrelieved by naproxen. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
why_right: The combination of infertility for 6 years and severe dysmenorrhea unrelieved by naproxen (NSAID failure) in a woman of 30 is the classic picture of endometriosis. Ectopic endometrial implants cause cyclic inflammatory pain and adhesions that distort tubal and ovarian anatomy, explaining the infertility. Primary dysmenorrhea usually responds to NSAIDs, so failure points to a secondary cause.
why_wrong_block:
A. Endometritis presents with fever, uterine tenderness and offensive discharge, typically after delivery, miscarriage or instrumentation; it is not a cause of long-standing cyclic pain.
B. Leiomyomata typically cause heavy menstrual bleeding and an enlarged irregular uterus; they can affect fertility, but severe NSAID-resistant dysmenorrhea with infertility is the endometriosis pattern.
D. Pelvic congestion syndrome causes chronic dull pelvic pain worse on prolonged standing, usually in multiparous women with pelvic varices; it is not linked to infertility.
key_concept:
Endometriosis = 3 Ds + infertility.
  • Dysmenorrhea (secondary, NSAID resistant), dyspareunia (deep), dyschezia
  • Exam: fixed retroverted uterus, uterosacral nodularity, adnexal mass (endometrioma)
  • Most common site: ovary
  • Diagnosis: laparoscopy (visual plus histology)
  • Adenomyosis: older multiparous, menorrhagia, diffusely enlarged tender uterus
exam_pearl: Severe dysmenorrhea + infertility = endometriosis; add menorrhagia and a boggy enlarged uterus in a multiparous woman and it becomes adenomyosis.
compiler_note:
Repeats: appears 2× in this file (also AS-0260).
Compiler note: Other version: 28-year-old, 6-year inability to conceive, severe dysmenorrhea not responding to NSAIDs; options Endometritis / PID / Endometriosis (highlighted) / PCOS.

stem: Pregnant lady at 12 weeks Her first pregnancy ended up with spontaneous abortion (they didn’t mention which trimester) Her 2nd pregnancy was uncomplicated, Her 3rd pregnancy had PPROM at 28 weeks, Presents with no complaints and normal examination, what is the most appropriate action?
OptC: Follow up in family medicine clinic
OptD: Follow in high risk clinics and close observation
why_right: Her history includes PPROM at 28 weeks, a previous spontaneous preterm birth, which makes this a high-risk pregnancy for recurrent preterm birth even though she is currently asymptomatic with a normal exam. She should be managed in a high-risk antenatal clinic with close surveillance (for example serial transvaginal cervical length and consideration of progesterone). There is no documented second-trimester painless loss, so she does not meet criteria for a history-indicated cerclage.
why_wrong_block:
A. An urgent cerclage is for an open cervix or a short cervix in a woman with prior second-trimester loss; she has no such loss documented, no symptoms and a normal exam, and PPROM is not cervical insufficiency.
B. Abdominal (transabdominal) cerclage is reserved for women whose previous transvaginal cerclage failed; she has never had a cerclage, and she is already pregnant, so a pre-pregnancy procedure is not possible.
C. Routine family medicine follow-up suits a low-risk woman; a prior preterm PPROM is a major risk factor for recurrence and needs specialist care.
key_concept:
Previous preterm birth or PPROM = high-risk antenatal follow-up.
  • History-indicated cerclage at 13 to 14 weeks: prior second-trimester painless loss (cervical insufficiency)
  • Prior loss presenting later: serial TVUS cervical length; cerclage if short before 24 weeks
  • No prior loss: cervical length screen; short cervix = vaginal progesterone
  • Abdominal cerclage: after a failed vaginal cerclage
  • Cerclage generally not placed after 24 weeks
exam_pearl: Painless second-trimester loss points to cerclage; a prior PPROM or preterm birth alone points to surveillance in a high-risk clinic.
